speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister, in view of the statement reported to have been made yesterday by him to the Canadian Labour Congress that every country of the commonwealth must be permitted to carry out its own policies internally without interference, whether he believes that this principle applies also to all other members of the United Nations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the observation I made yesterday had to do with the statement in the brief presented by the C.L.C., which read as follows:
To say the least, we feel extremely uncomfortable in the same company with the government of South Africa, and would favour its exclusion from the councils of the commonwealth of nations.
The observation I made at that time was this; that the commonweath is representative of countries in various stages of democratic advancement, and that I would not support any action to exclude from the councils of the commonwealth of nations the Union of South Africa, regardless of my strong feelings in respect of discrimination.
With regard to the question asked as to the difference between the commonwealth and the United Nations, I think the answer is apparent when some consideration is given to the membership of the United Nations and the membership of the commonwealth. So far as the commonwealth is concerned, it is a voluntary organization joined together by those principles which are generally accepted as the British heritage.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. I do not think the Prime Minister dealt with my question as to whether the same principle would have to be applied under the United Nations charter to every member of the United Nations as would have to be applied to members of the commonwealth at the United Nations.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext:
I would think the application of the principles of the United Nations charter
79951-0-324
was not a matter falling under the administrative responsibility of the Prime Minister. It seems to me that the question as put ranges beyond the administrative responsibility of the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: The Prime Minister has kindly given us clarification of one of the statements he made yesterday on this matter, and I should now like to ask him a question with regard to another statement he made yesterday on the same subject. Does the Prime Minister now wish to reconsider the statement he made yesterday that the apartheid question in South Africa is not one that he would like to see brought up, or see discussed, at the meeting of prime ministers next May? Does the Prime Minister not think that in view of the character of these meetings, their secrecy, this is among the kind of questions that should be and have been discussed among the prime ministers of the commonwealth?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext:
I have not the transcript of my remarks before me, and the hon. gentleman is reading from a press statement. What I stated was simply this, that I would not bring before the prime ministers' conference, or indeed support, any action that would exclude the Union of South Africa from the councils of the commonwealth of nations.
I know the hon. gentleman wants to be helpful. If he were in the position of prime minister, with his regard for the commonwealth, I wonder whether he or his leader would support exclusion.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: No one supports the exclusion of any member of the commonwealth. The question was not exclusion but discussion.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: Oh, no; there was no reference other than to the matter of exclusion, which is a course I would not accept. I think, from the hon. gentleman's statement, that he joins with me in holding that view.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext: In view of the clarification which the right hon. gentleman has just given may I ask him, then, whether we are to understand that he would not oppose any discussion of this matter at a prime ministers' conference such as the one he will attend next May?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER TO LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext:
There is no agenda in the ordinary sense of the word at prime ministers' conferences. Matters are discussed
Inquiries of the Ministry there; decisions are not made. Those things which affect the various parts of the commonwealth, both internal matters and external relations, are discussed. In my experience-and it is a short one, for I have attended only one conference, though I have read the reports of all previous conferences -there are no vetoes on discussion.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FREE VOTE AND DISCUSSION
speechtext: If I am not mistaken that question was asked earlier in the session and dealt with. speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FREE VOTE AND DISCUSSION
speechtext: I did ask that question on the orders of the day, and I think the Prime Minister said the matter had not been decided and would be given consideration. Is it not appropriate to ask, a week or ten days later, what has been the result of that consideration?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FREE VOTE AND DISCUSSION
speechtext:
At first blush it seems a highly improper question, to ask any hon. member to allow members to vote freely in this house. It is a principle of our proceedings that hon. members decide themselves how they are to vote. It is a reflection on the house to suggest -that anybody will tell them how to vote.
If hon. members will hear me out without further noise or interruption I will go on to state that in so far as voting is a matter of party restraint or influenced by party decisions, then it is a party matter and not one of the administrative responsibility of a minister of the crown. It seems to me in those circumstances that this is not a proper question to raise on the orders of the day, because it does not relate to administrative responsibility nor to the business of the house.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FREE VOTE AND DISCUSSION
speechtext: Your Honour is correct in saying it is a principle, but unfortunately it is not a fact. Therefore may I ask the question in a different way. Will the Prime Minister inform the house as to when a decision will be made as to a free vote, and will it be done-

speechtext: Then I should like to ask this question. When that question was asked some ten days ago it was allowed and an answer was given to the effect that it was under consideration. Why was it allowed then and not now?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport arising out of the fears of the maritime ports about winter navigation in the St. Lawrence. Can the minister report on recent icebreaking activity in the Montreal area?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Government icebreakers are operating in the Montreal area of the St. Lawrence river solely for the purpose of flood control. Several days ago abnormally high water levels caused by ice jams submerged some wharves and roadways, and flooded the basement floor of at least one elevator. The national harbours board requested the Department of Transport to provide icebreakers to relieve this acute and damaging situation.
The operation of the icebreakers earlier than usual this year is due entirely to the fact that the flood conditions occurred earlier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport arising out of the answer he has just given, in which he has indicated that the icebreakers which are now being used for icebreaking operations into Montreal are being used for the purpose of assisting in the prevention of floods.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: My question is this. In view of the fact that the minister has already stated that winter navigation would be assisted in the various ports of the lower St. Lawrence up as far as Quebec, a statement which he made in Montebello, Que., how does he reconcile the statement which he then made with the answer he has given to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert this morning?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: That is very simple, as the hon. member knows because he held this portfolio for a number of years. Every year for many years it has been necessary to break a channel to allow the flood waters to get out of the Montreal area so they will not flood the area, part of which is represented by the hon. member, and I know he has professed great interest in having these flood waters released. This has been going on for many years. There is no change, and the hon. member knows all this perfectly well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: But my question to the minister was this. Why did he say that winter navigation would be provided right up to the port of Quebec?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking at Baie Comeau I said that we were going to try to keep navigation open on the north shore to provide that area, which has no railway service, with an outlet for its goods and an inlet for its supplies during the winter season.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his clarification, but I wish he would clarify it .a little more. I have his words here. He


said "right up to the port of Quebec". How does he reconcile that with the answer he has given to the member?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Where are those words found?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Here is what the minister said on January 22, 1958:
With this group of ships available it should be possible within the next few years-
That was in 1958 and we are now in 1960. -to meet virtually all requirements on the St. Lawrence and gulf areas including such winter shipping as may wish to proceed into the various ports in the lower St. Lawrence even as far up as Quebec.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
That is exactly what we are
doing this year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Thank you. That is a complete contradiction.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY

speechtext: Yes, you said it here.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: I did not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: It is all here in black and white.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: I did not.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the hon. member for Laurier was, I think, trying to convince the house that I had made a statement in this house in 1958 dealing with winter navigation into Quebec.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Order, please. Is the hon. member rising on a point of order?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I am rising on a question of privilege in order to clear up what was said.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
What the hon. member for
Laurier was quoting was a speech in this house by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), who was quoting a speech by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Tasse), supposedly made in Montreal, who was quoting a speech that I am supposed to have made in 1958. I have no recollection of ever having said those things.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I expected this answer so I went down to my office to get the speech. It is a fact that this speech was delivered by the hon. member for Quebec East.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Oh, yes; I should be allowed to answer what the minister has said. This is what was said.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: If the hon. member thinks it is relevant to the question of privilege to read what the minister said, I shall allow him to do so.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The only portion I am going to read are the words of the minister as quoted by the hon. member for Quebec East. This is what was said by the minister:
With this groups of ships available, it should be possible, within the next few years, to meet virtually all requirements on the St. Lawrence and gulf areas, including such winter shipping as may wish to proceed to the various ports in the lower St. Lawrence, even as far up as Quebec.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: The words are "up as far as" but not including.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Hoist on his own petard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: I think the point of privilege has been sufficiently aired.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ICE- BREAKING ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. If the Minister of Finance has anything to say, let him say it here and now.

speechtext: That might be a point of order, but perhaps the hon. member will address himself to the chair if he finds anybody in the house misconducting himself.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a supplementary question to the question asked the Minister of Transport about St. Lawrence shipping. speechtext:
I had the
honour yesterday, Mr. Speaker, to present the usual congratulations which are offered on such an occasion as this, and now I should like to continue my remarks in relation to the speech from the throne.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to represent in this house a constituency whose history is one of the richest as far as national events are concerned. The constituency of St. James, when it was still the heart of the Montreal East division, at the very beginning of confederation, elected to represent it in this house none other than Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, Sir John A. Macdonald's French Canadian partner.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would allow me to interrupt him to ask for some attention on the part of the house. There are a great many private conversations going on in too loud a voice, and I hope hon. members will give the hon. member for St. James the courtesy of a good hearing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. (Translation):
Cartier had the courage of seeing far afield, as regards the province of Quebec, when he did not hesitate to join his efforts to those of Macdonald to give birth to this great country to which we are all proud of belonging today.
The constituency of St. James, located in the very heart of the metropolis of the province of Quebec and of Canada, has been closely linked in the course of the last century, with the epic of Canadian confederation, and has shared its times of hardship and of greatness.
Designed to achieve the combination of the live forces of both east and west, of Lower and Upper Canada, of Quebec and Ontario and the maritimes, of the French and English races-in order to ensure the glorious expan-
The Address-Mr. Campeau sion of Canada towards the promising west- confederation, in respecting the fundamental rights of both great races, at the birth of our country, and through special arrangements balancing the development opportunities of all partners, great and small, confederation, as I say, managed to produce, in less than a century, a strong and integrated nation, while a thousand years of history could not do better in the case of many European nations.
Since 1867, Canada has known an unheard and undreamt expansion, surpassing the most ambitious dreams of both Cartier and Macdonald. The original four partners are now ten, the newcomers carving a place for themselves out of large areas of the continent, while northward, vast expanses of nearly illimited dimensions are now opening up to the appetite of giant new provinces in process of formation.
This phenomenal expansion did not take place without raising increasing problems of growth and development, which Canadians must now face, because the Liberal administration of the last 20 years preferred to rely on a policy of complacency, rather than demand the necessary sacrifices from the people.
Foremost among those problems, is that of urbanization, as evidenced by the appearance, from coast to coast, of villages, towns and cities which are ruthlessly devouring forests, plains, mountains and, today, even the northern tundra. An increasing population is ceaselessly demanding housing, in increasing number, and multiplying social security problems. Urbanization and expansion call for rapid and extended transport facilities, as well as increasing public works to cope with the complexity of new needs. Because of giant productivity, limited consumption has not always been able to absorb production, giving rise to seasonal unemployment and its ill-effects. All those problems call for increasing capital investments to support the physical and economic structure of the country, and to allow the nation to meet the increasing obligations it has to assume in the international sphere.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that we must now reconsider the Canadian confederation, and I must express admiration for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has indicated his intention of starting by repatriating the constitution. There is today, as there was in 1867, the same urgent need to combine the live forces of east and west, of the two original races and of the many others who have been added to them since, the first partners and the new giants of the far west, and there is also need

The Address-Mr. Campeau for new special arrangements to balance the chances of development of the ten partners, large and small, so as to favour another great and glorious rush to the beckoning north, but more particularly a bold and deep rush into the very core of our economic structure, providing an adequate solution for those new needs that emerged during the last century, like urbanization, social security, external trade, international relations and, last, but not least, industrialization.
The greatest need of Canadian confederation at the start of this decade which will mark its centenary, is for a policy of national development, designed to provide a bridge between economic interests, just as in earlier days rapid communications bridged geographical distances.
It is to that end that the Prime Minister, who has made national unity his life goal, has always put forward measures to promote a national development program designed to stimulate private industry and enable it to co-operate with the government in the enrichment of our national heritage.
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of St. James and the province of Quebec will not hesitate to do their share in the implementation of that program, and thus to take their rightful place in the Canadian confederation, in the same spirit as Quebec displayed in 1867, when it responded so generously to Sir Georges Etienne Cartier's call for national unity, for one Canada and one Canadian nation.
The province of Quebec has recognized that same spirit in this statement from the present Prime Minister:
We are for confederation because of the varied elements which make up the Canadian nation, because of the rights and liberties they enjoy under the constitution, because of the equal respect for our two great cultures, and because of the powers which Cartier and Macdonald sought to preserve for each Canadian province.
No Liberal leader, Mr. Speaker, has ever had the courage to come out with such a clear-cut and definite statement.
As the keeper of the most sacred traditions of the Canadian nation, the province of Quebec insists on respect for confederation, without which Canada would not exist today. The citizens of Quebec, being aware of the obligations arising out of confederation, would be unhappy if development lagged behind in some parts of the national territory or in sections of Canada's economy, and as in the past, they will not hesitate to

accept the sacrifices needed to insure the progress and full development of the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, since the end of world war II, Canada has experienced unprecedented development. That development has mainly reflected itself in a year by year rise in capital investment, and has therefore resulted in a rapid expansion of our production facilities. Unfortunately, through some unexplainable and inexcusable lack of foresight and economic planning on the part of the Liberal administration, that expansion was not always in line with the trends in our external trade and with our domestic consumption. The gap between production and consumption resulted in seasonal unemployment for which the Liberal government can hardly deny its responsibility.
No doubt we could not pay ourselves for manufacturing goods that we cannot use or sell. Nor could we pay ourselves for any length of time at least, for producing nothing. Unemployment insurance is not and cannot be a substitute for work.
During the postwar period, the Liberal administration resorted to taxation calculated to produce substantial "surpluses", under the pretence of thus warding off inflation. The facts have shown that a monetary policy alone cannot check the inflationary increase of wages, of production costs and of consumer prices or check rising economic trends.
A large volume of foreign capital, many requests for increases in wages and profits, changes affecting foreign trade, the rate of new capital investments and the general taxation structure, are all factors which were added to the problems of money volume and interest rates, and affected the trends of the Canadian economy, unnoticed by the Liberal administration in suspended animation, and led to the recession out of which we emerged victoriously as a result of the firm and drastic efforts of this Conservative government.
Due to the rapid post-war expansion, the economy of the country could meet, without the Liberal government having anything to do with it, the needs resulting from the war, the necessities of conversion, a considerable increase in immigration and a great number of drastic changes in our way of living.
It should be noted however that the uncontrolled rate of expansion has created employment in fields of activity which we could not maintain and which prevented other and more stable activities to increase employment.

Such a situation no doubt did not contribute to stable employment. The Liberal government, making no real effort to correct the situation, was gradually leading us towards inflation and to the bankruptcy of individuals who could no longer adjust their revenues to the increasing costs and to major changes in industries unable to compete at home and abroad.
The Liberal administration did not seem and does not seem as yet to have understood that the choice was not between total employment and stable prices, but should have consisted in a national development policy which would have produced a real economic growth, giving work to labourers, increasing production and consumption, while maintaining them in balance, and finally thus improving our living standard without draining our natural resources.
Even if today we have to pay the price for that development, which went on uncontrolled during the 22 years of Liberal rule, Canada in 1960 remains a prosperous country in spite of everything. The prophets of doom sitting on the other side of the house do not seem to get over the fact that Canada, in 1960, after three years of Conservative rule, is enjoying a more flourishing economy than it has ever known.
What was lacking in Canada until now, because the Liberal system never thought of giving it to this country or perhaps did not have the courage to do so, is a positive economic policy, tending to the rapid development of our manufacturing industry, so as to depend less on foreign countries and offer more employment to our people, while trying to increase our population, which would lower our production costs by adequately developing our domestic market.
There have been two main failings: first of all a too slow progress in our manufacturing industry, which partly explains the persistence of unemployment and the increasing dependence of our economy on the fluctuations of our foreign trade.
The importance of the manufacturing industry, as a dynamic force in Canadian economy does not rest solely upon the fact that it gives direct employment to 26 per cent of Canadian workers and is the industry most productive of wealth for seven provinces out of ten, but more particularly upon the fact that it is capable of bringing about the high level of economic activity which is the basis of national prosperity.
The Address-Mr. Campeau
The prospects of greater industrialization are more encouraging than ever, especially in those industries that are able to produce locally at a competitive price what we would otherwise import and be unable to export.
The role of the federal government is to shape its general policies, and particularly its economic policy, in such a way as to ensure the prosperity of the nation as a whole and of every province at the same time.
There are several ways in which the government can do this. It can be either by way of the tax structure, or through tariffs arising out of international agreements, through credit facilities or again through research. In the performance of this task, the federal government must not substitute itself for the provinces or for the municipalities.
In the international sphere, the Liberal administration has not always had a clear perception of Canada's interests, and all too often, it discharged Canada's international obligations without taking account of the country's national needs.
Even on the national scene, the Liberal administration never had the wisdom to draw up a general plan based on Canada's resources, productive capacity and local needs.
The Liberal administration, for purely political reasons, too hastily and too extensively converted the wonderful development of the country into a betterment of the material standard of living, and into expenditures for consumer goods, while other things much more urgent and much more important called for the drastic action of the federal authorities.
Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to have definite economic goals, to have concrete plans for the expansion and guidance of our economy. We should, as soon as possible, set up some kind of control and industrial promotion organization so that the development of the country follows a comprehensive plan, maintaining a fair balance in the development of our natural resources and in the distribution of our foreign trade, through the use of our physical and human resources in areas and industries where productivity is greater, consolidating and expanding foreign trade and making it possible for the powers of private enterprise to support the growing trend through a stable currency and investment of public funds where they can use the expansion of national production for the stabilization of economic conditions.
At this point I want to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) for his leadership in setting up an

The Address-Mr. Campeau advisory committee of experts to study the problems of foreign and internal trade and of industrial development. Concerning the latter, the committee will seek to determine the fields of activity where new industries could take advantage of new opportunities made available on the local market by the increase of population and of imports, and efficiently compete at home as well as abroad. This is certainly a huge step in the right direction.
However, I feel that this initiative must be followed immediately by a complementary one in the field of action. It is urgent, indeed, to set up in Canada an organization for industry just as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was established at a time when the country was going through a housing crisis.
The need for industrialization is as pressing now, Mr. Speaker, and an appropriate machinery is needed to insure orderly development.
The main purpose of such an organization, which could be called the Canadian industrial development corporation, would be to guarantee and make loans for the establishment of new industries and for the protection and development of existing industries. It could absorb or be integrated with the industrial development bank set up in 1944, whose main purpose was to correct an anomaly of our financial system which offers no facilities for meeting the needs of risk capital in the field of industrial development. Its activity was limited to small loans and to certain categories of industries established by legislation.
The operations of the proposed corporation would be self-sustaining in the long run. The amount of research required to establish a plan of action could be made through existing departments, which would proportionately reduce launching costs.
The new organization would base its operations on a national development program aiming at the development of our natural resources, the proper distribution of our industrial potential, as well as of our population and its needs, the adequate distribution of manufactured products, and taking into account our domestic and external trade, transport facilities, our northern territories and other similar factors.
It would have to undertake a complete survey of the present situation and analyse the means of conserving and enlarging existing industries and of creating new ones, so as to ensure the orderly development of our national economy. The result would be an

integrated program of economic and industrial expansion in definite stages. Each individual loan would be made in the light of those general basic factors, according to a procedure similar to that now applied by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the case of housing.
That program is linked with various other national problems. It would, first of all, be an extraordinary help in the field of technical and professional education, by giving our specialized students facilities for training and possibilities of employment. We could thus keep our scientists in Canada and avoid their going to the United States, as was the case under the Liberal rule, when, from 1951 to 1956, about 3,000 engineers and 800 scientists left us in this way. The considerable sums of money we are spending on scientific education should certainly not benefit the United States more than Canada.
That program would facilitate the establishment of a sound immigration policy. The new immigrants would be absorbed by the new industries and would thus create an adequate market for increased local production.
The program would also have the effect of speeding up the development of territories in the far north, which is being intensively pursued by the present Conservative government.
The program, in conjunction with a wise tariff policy, would also result in balancing our trade with foreign countries. We could reduce imports by developing local industries to meet local needs, with corresponding benefits in the form of greater employment opportunities, higher local tax revenues, more purchases of local materials and equipment, and greater profits and dividends leading up to new formation of Canadian capital.
New products could be manufactured and consumed locally or exported at a profit. The necessary research would have considerable influence on the training and employment of Canadian technicians and on the use of our local material resources.
Advanced technology, based on research, is a dominant force in a highly industrialized community. Technological research can create new employment opportunities by opening up new markets. That, probably, is the most important single factor for Canada's future industrial development.
Finally, the program would have considerable effect on cyclical unemployment, which a scientifically based industrial production and expansion plan could reduce to a strict minimum.

A program such as this would enable Canada to effectively resist the European economic blocs, particularly the communist bloc, and the impact of increasing industrialization in underdeveloped countries.
The activities of such a body would be concerned with our industrial potential and the requirements of consumption. The first approach is linked with labour and employment problems, with production capacity and available markets. The second approach concerns expenditures of revenues, available goods and services and utilization of resources.
The consumption requirements of the Canadian people, would be surveyed, as they occur in various possible conditions and, as they develop-according to a given national income geographically distributed-and at a determined frequency.
An outline of industrial potential would be of interest to all those affected by industry. The combination of both surveys would permit a more efficient utilization of our human and material resources, while maintaining the economic equilibrium of our	national
prosperity.
The information thus gathered would be useful in several fields. In planning new industries or in enlarging existing ones, businessmen usually have at their disposal excellent information about immediate technical and economical problems. However, this is an extremely difficult process for them, because they do not have the facilities nor the required means of ascertaining the complex general conditions in which their industry has to be integrated. Inaccurate estimates of consumer demand and of the existing industrial potential too often result in unfavourable economic losses to individual producers and to the community as a whole.
It is on the basis of such fundamental research that it would be possible to establish a program of economic balance which would permit an orderly and continuous growth for the whole of Canada.
The success of the plan I have just described, Mr. Speaker, will depend to a great extent on the co-ordination of efforts, on the intensity and depth of research and on soundly based economic forecasts.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is again experiencing growing pains. The present situation calls for magnitude, breadth of view, magnitude of intention and magnitude of efforts. It is up to us Canadians to take up the challenge.
The Address-Mr. Campeau
Canada, facing the fast rate of economic and technological developments, and the rapid rise of living standards, must change its traditional stand and adapt itself to an economy of abundance affected by the repeated impact of excessively rapid and successive changes.
We must realize that we have all joined into a common venture whose basic purpose is to insure orderly national development and thus achieve the maximum stability of economic growth. The success of such an undertaking is vitally and almost solely dependent on the close co-operation of all Canadians.
The Prime Minister is the man to obtain such vital co-operation within Canadian unity. The national development program which he has put into implementation tends to ensure the progress of our country's economy, according to a gradual and wise course, while remaining deeply rooted in Canadian traditions, but traditions enriched by the requirements of the present. Relying on the philosophy of the common man, he ignores Liberal and C.C.F.'s doctrinaire theories and considers, first of all, human values the most important of all. Hence, its middle-of-the-road approach, sparing Canadians both leftist and rightist radical excesses, in which the opposition groups too readily indulge.
The Conservative government, Mr. Speaker, has acquired, still has and will keep the confidence of the man in the street, on account of its respect for fundamental values, such as individual initiative, freedom of private enterprise, limited governmental control and, above all, national unity in equality of races, languages, religions and opportunities.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I recall words of the Hon. Paul Sauve, the late premier of the province of Quebec, to whom the constituency of St. James wishes to pay tribute as it does to his predecessor-both of whom died on the job-while at the same time wishing health and success to their successor, the Hon. Paul Sauve delivered the following message on the occasion of New Year's day:
Judging from the great promises of the future, it seems that conditions have never been better for united action and for progress and co-operation. Let us keep closely united, so that our hopes of today may become the achievements of tomorrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel rather at a loss this morning, because I have listened to so many members

The Address-Mr. Houck all persons in all walks of life. In like manner they, as citizens of this wonderful country of ours, must have salaries which will enable them to buy these essentials of life without having to resort either to having their wives work in order to keep the table supplied or having to carry on "moonlighting" which is, I believe, the term applied to those who have a spare time occupation.
This is an old saying; many hon. members have heard it stated:
For many years it has been generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service. First the salaries must be enough to do the job, that is to attract the right kind of men and women into the service and keep them in it; second, they must be fair as between civil servants and people outside the service, the taxpayers if you will, which means that the salaries we pay for any class of work should be comparable with those paid by private employers for similar classes of work, taking into account the other terms of employment that are necessary to make a fair comparison. I think these principles should continue to guide us.
I know civil servants would be satisfied if they could have these three things:
1.	A number of representatives of staff meet with an equal number of responsible representatives of government who are empowered to make decisions.
2.	The meeting to be chaired by a civil service commissioner who shall have no voting power but shall offer advice to the negotiators.
3.	Matters upon which agreement cannot be reached shall be submitted to arbitration, with the decision of the arbitrator binding to both sides.
In many meetings they have had with the civil service-and I refer to the government *-I feel that the main issue for these people is that they are anxious to obtain bargaining rights with arbitration, such as are enjoyed by civil servants in many other countries, so that in the future they will not have to resort to the cup in hand approach and be subject to the whims of political expedience of the government in power. I certainly would not like to see this government, or any government, glued to a policy which would identify it as a cheap employer, which would scare away from government service persons who are highly educated, with various skills and with very high standards of character. Fair pay in the civil service is certainly the only principle by which Canada can maintain a high calibre of civil servant. Cheap employees in the civil service would to me be the same as a mediocre ball player trying to play in the big league.
I would be remiss at this time if I did not pay my respects to the customs and immigration officers in my riding who are performing such a wonderful job. They are called upon, especially in summertime, to interview

thousands and thousands of people crossing the border, and naturally in the tourist months they face a very strenuous season. But I have heard nothing but praise for these officers. Many tourists enter Canada for the first time and their first impression is their lasting impression, and if they get a good first impression they carry it throughout their trip in Canada.
I would also like to pay my respects to the many R.C.M.P. we have at the border, and to the agriculture employees-indeed all the civil servants-especially those of the post office, who performed such a miraculous job not only in my riding but I presume in all ridings of hon. members in this house during the Christmas rush.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring before this house a very pertinent point, and in doing this I would appreciate it if the hon. members of this house would realize that I am bringing forth this argument not on behalf of the Liberal party, or any other association, but I am bringing it before the house because of my long standing in politics. I make this statement-naturally I assume responsibility for it as a member of this house-and make it as the thought of Bill Houck and Bill Houck alone. I make this statement, indeed, with some boldness; that I think the time has arrived when we in this house should give some consideration to compulsory voting. I am going to ask the Prime Minister, through his good offices, along with the cabinet council, seriously to consider setting up a small committee of this house, indeed a non-partisan committee, to study this question from all angles. If it achieves no other purpose than to make the people more vote conscious I believe we would have made a great stride forward toward bringing up the percentage of those who vote at election time at any of the three levels of government.
When the hon. members of this house or the members of any provincial legislature or municipal council consider how much money it cost them to try and get the vote out on election day, and then only a small percentage of voters turn out, it is indeed most discouraging. When we realize-and I know other hon. members have the same trouble as I-the vast amount of money we have to spend on election day, not only for people making telephone calls but for hiring of cars, etc., I think it is a shame in this day of democracy that we have to almost get down on bended knee to beg the people to go out and exercise their franchise.
Another point which almost drives me crazy on election day is the fact that as members we get many calls from people left off the voting lists. We are not to blame;

it is the voter himself. It is absolutely im-posssible for the candidate to see that everybody is on the voting list. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, if some of these people who fail to exercise their sacred right of the franchise lived behind the iron curtain and had to vote, or perhaps better said, were told how to vote, they would realize the privileges which exist in a democracy. Mr. Speaker, I state very frankly, and I truly mean this, that I would far rather be defeated with a 95 per cent vote cast on election day than be elected with only a 30 per cent or 40 per cent vote cast. I would then feel that the people had spoken and I was either wanted or not wanted.
I think most of the people of our dominion do not realize how the candidates running for election give up not only their time but their money to see to it that a good vote is cast. I would like to pay my respects at this time to the various organizations, especially the junior chambers of commerce, throughout the Dominion of Canada who always run a campaign to get the voters out on election day. I often ask people when they come to see me in my office whether they had taken the trouble to vote. I always say to them, "I do not want to know how you voted, so please do not tell me". But I do say, "Did you take the trouble to go out on election day?" I have kept track of the answers, and I find that over 60 per cent of the people who come to see me to complain about the government or to ask for jobs or to ask for favours of some sort, have said to me, "No, I did not take the trouble to go out to vote".
I think if a non-partisan committee was set up, as I have suggested, it would make the people more vote conscious and get them thinking that they should exercise their right to the franchise. If such a committee were set up it could call before it the chief electoral officer of each province and hear some of their recommendations. They could also call some of the clerks of the municipalities, especially the large municipalities, and any other organizations in this regard. I think if they appeared before this committee they could tell the committee, either pro or con, what they think about compulsory voting. After a complete study of this question I realize that some leniency would have to be granted, especially at the advance polls.
I challenge businessmen, Mr. Speaker, to devote the same long and careful consideration and study to the election of their elected representatives that they employ in the employment of company officials; for certainly their public servants, in what they do in government service or in an elected office, have as much to do with shaping their
The Address-Mr. Houck future and that of their businesses as the president or other officers in their own great organizations.
It has always been a puzzle to me why rural districts have a larger percentage of voters turn out than urban or suburban areas. I think it is the urban group who really do not get out to vote, but then after election they will storm the municipal council hall, or even the elected member's house, with criticism in some form or another. This, to me, shows that they are interested in themselves only, because they do not vote for who they think should represent them. Perhaps they did not like the personnel of the council or ballot, and did not choose to go out and exercise their right of the franchise; but to me they have neglected their responsibility, which is the birthright of every voter.
I quite well recall that in a municipal election last December a few miles from Niagara Falls-I admit I am ashamed of this-the people had to go less than a mile to vote, and only an 18 per cent vote was cast on election day. Naturally there is generally greater interest in a federal election, but the percentage is not enough to express the will of the people. In the 1945 federal election 76 per cent of the people turned out to vote; in 1949, the figure was 74 per cent; in 1953, 67 per cent; in 1957, 74 per cent; and in 1958, 79 per cent.
I think this committee could study from all angles the commonwealth electoral act, 1918-1934, of Australia, where they have compulsory voting. There are many clauses in this act. I have not read them all, but a penalty is provided for not voting, albeit a small one. Perhaps I might read section 12 (a) of that act, which says:
-fails to vote at an election without a valid and sufficient reason for such failure; or, (b) on receipt of a notice in accordance with subsection (4) of this section, fails to fill up, sign, and post within the time allowed under subsection (5) of this section the form (duly witnessed) which is attached to the notice.
The form mentioned there is the one they have to fill out to explain why they did not vote. If they did not vote, then according to the act they are fined not less than ten shillings and not more than two pounds. I think extensive study of this question of voting, whether it was made compulsory or not, would increase the total percentage of votes cast on election day. I talked to one of the men in the Australian embassy, and he told me that since they had introduced compulsory voting in that country in 1915-and this does not imply attendance at the polls, because they are very lenient, especially with regard to mailing in votes at advance polls-they had found the system had produced an average

The Address-Mr. Houck poll of more than 90 per cent of the registered voters, as compared with 50 per cent when voting was optional. They had also discovered, as we, of course, would discover, that under compulsory voting there were many more spoiled ballots.
I am very serious in raising this matter of compulsory voting, and I repeat that I hope hon. members will be fair enough with me- and I know they will-to realize that this is my personal feeling with regard to this vastly important subject. I think our citizens should interest themselves in government because, when we consider the question, we are all stockholders in the government and, indeed, in the Dominion of Canada, and we receive our dividends through the services that are afforded.
I repeat that in my view a committee should be set up so that a thorough study might be made of the Australian commonwealth election act. Representations from all interested parties, whether they were for or against compulsory voting, would at least bring about a bigger percentage of votes cast at election time and would certainly make citizens more vote conscious. It stands to reason that a voter who fails to exercise his franchise eventually penalizes himself, and I think those individuals who fail to exercise the franchise and then sit back and criticize the incumbents of office who fail to do what he considers they should do, should lose the right to criticize.
We realize, of course, that it is impossible to bludgeon an individual into exercising his franchise, but it should be forcibly brought home to such people that the right to vote in a democratic country is a great responsibility which was acquired in ages past by great sacrifice on the part of our forefathers, who in some instances fought and died for this privilege.
Persons elected to public office have, of necessity, a difficult job to do if public affairs are to be properly and sincerely administered. There is, of course, a very great danger that should there be a continuance of this complete apathy on the part of the electors there could eventually arise a form of dictatorship, or some communist form of government. In my home city, with regard to municipal elections, this same condition of apathy exists and is clearly evident, since within the past ten years the percentage of votes cast at municipal elections, has ranged from a low of 28.2 per cent to a high of 55.3 per cent. The high point was reached when there were a couple of money questions before the people and they were asked to vote for a mayor.
Various suggestions have been made as to what could be done to prevent this condition


and bring about an improvement in the percentage of votes cast. I repeat that I believe this could best be done through a committee which would receive publicity and make the people more vote conscious. Correction will only come about when there is concerted action throughout the dominion to convey to the elector that he has a stake in his community, his province and his dominion, and that he must protect his stake by exercising his franchise and thus attempt to obtain the services of men of the highest calibre. Concerted action is also needed to bring home to individual electors that they need to keep fully informed on current affairs so that in the event that they themselves are elected to office they may carry out their duties in the most efficient and desirable manner.
I think it should be the ultimate goal of every member of this house who is interested in this subject to see that the electors should take interest in this God-given privilege and act upon it; and I sincerely hope, in closing, that the Prime Minister will see fit to appoint a small, non-partisan committee at least to study this great question.
In closing I should be remiss indeed if I did not pass on to hon. members warm personal regards and a friendly hello from my colleague the hon. member of Welland (Mr. McMillan), who has been ill and who will not be able to return to the house until possibly some time in April. On his behalf I wish to convey greetings to all hon. members of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been my pleasure this week and since the start of this throne speech debate to listen to the constructive ideas advanced from many quarters of this house dealing with matters that are of vital interest to the house and to the people of Canada.
At this time I should like to join in the tributes paid by hon. members from all sides to the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address. May I say that the manner in which the hon. gentleman and the charming lady acquitted themselves was a credit to this chamber and to our best traditions.
May I also extend to you, sir, my congratulations upon your appointment to the

high office you now hold. From all the evidence it is apparent that you will fill that position in the best tradition.
With your permission and that of hon. members of this house I should like to deal for a few moments with the riding I have had the honour to represent since 1952. It is only on rare occasions that a minister of the crown has an opportunity to say something about the riding which he represents. With your indulgence I wish to say that the conditions in Ontario riding, both in the agricultural and industrial sectors, give me cause for pride because there is an unprecedented buoyancy in the economy of my riding.
The people in my riding are earning more, spending more and saving more. Business generally is very good. Our population is increasing, particularly in our industrial areas of Oshawa, Whitby and Ajax. These are the main urban centres of my riding. The population of the city of Oshawa has more than doubled in the past ten years. One thing of which we are especially proud in the city of Oshawa is that home ownership in that community where I have lived for 39 years is approximately 85 per cent. That is indeed an enviable record and something that we rejoice in.
Because of the location of General Motors of Canada in Oshawa-which is known as the motor city of Canada-people from all over the dominion flock to the area in order to secure jobs. The automobile industry in the past number of years has experienced its best years of productivity. More people are employed now by the automobile industry than ever before and this, I feel, reflects on the whole economy throughout Canada.
We have excellent harbour facilities in Oshawa and Whitby and this augurs well for the industrial expansion of this area particularly in relation to the St. Lawrence seaway. Hon. members will have noticed that in the speech from the throne mention was made of the fact that a bill will be presented to this house to establish a harbour commission in the city of Oshawa. This is a forward step which will help to enlarge facilities and provide for the future development of the harbour area of the city of Oshawa.
Industry is inquiring continually for locations in this area and many are locating there. As a result, the population is growing. But all this stems in the main from good municipal government. I am proud to say that in my own riding-in all our municipal councils-good judgment has been shown in the management of municipal affairs. They are aware that it is necessary to plan for the future. Their enthusiasm is of the highest
The Address-Mr. Starr order. The people in my riding work with an eye to the future and with a sense of confidence in what they are doing.
I now turn to matters that are of pressing concern to all Canadians. Yesterday the Canadian Labour Congress presented a brief to the government. In view of certain allegations which have been made and certan fears that have been expressed-I refer particularly to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and also by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)-I should like to make some comments in this regard. I regret that the hon. member for Essex East is not here today. I realize he had to keep an appointment to which he was previously committed.
We have not had in this session to the same extent we had in the last the spectacle of the hon. member for Essex East rising in his place with his prophecies of doom and despair. However, he has made references on orders of the day. He has implied here in the house and to the people of Canada that the situation is somewhat less favourable than it has been reported to be by those who are concerned with questions of business and economics. In spite of the hopeful situation that is revealed in the light of the facts the hon. gentleman has continued to convey an impression of doom and despair.
If the hon. member has shown perhaps a lessened tendency towards doom and despair this session I think his change of heart is understandable in view of the evidence that the recession has been overcome and that the measures taken by this government have been effective. Nevertheless in recent utterances he has still managed, as I mentioned a moment ago, to create the impression that defeatism and pessimism are his stock in trade and the stock in trade of his particular group. The hon. gentleman interprets the role of his group as harbingers of gloom and that, I think, is becoming commonly known.
I would refer the hon. member for Essex East to the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress which was presented to the government yesterday. In their brief they underscore that attitude of defeatism and pessimism as a danger to our economy and our national welfare. The authors of this brief are clear-thinking people and I feel they have their finger on the public pulse. I refer the hon. gentleman to other matters of interest in that very able presentation and quote from a reference on page 14 of the Canadian Labour Congress brief which reads as follows:
Your government has taken certain measures which helped to lift us out of the recession. For example, you ran a large deficit partly for that purpose. We urge you to finish the job.
512	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Starr
I refer particularly to the last sentence of that quotation. That is exactly what this government proposes to do. We propose to finish the job.
We heard much about unemployment in the last session of parliament. We heard about the hungry days of the thirties and were told that worse was yet to come. Let us examine exactly what has happened. It seems to me that everyone in this country is aware that the recession is over except members opposite.
May I refer again to the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress. This reference will be found at page 12:
The economic situation is better than when we met you a year ago. Production is up, unemployment is down.
They go on to point out certain factors in the economy which cause them some anxiety, and I am sure that if the hon. member for Essex East were here he would note this and make the most of these passages. In any case, Mr. Speaker, wherever you look, to labour, management, the economists, the picture is the same, namely one of economic growth and expansion throughout our country.
The other night the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) quoted extensively from the presidents of the chartered banks, those impartial witnesses whom the hon. member for Essex East called upon so exhaustively last session but upon whom he has not called this session. They agree that the recession is over.
