speechtext:
He has not spoken but I am sure if he does speak he will not refer to what they say about our economy this year. They all agree the recession is over.
Let us turn to another testimony, that of Mr. Raymond Daniell, writing in the Economic and Business Review of the New York Times. Looking over the Canadian scene, Mr. Daniell found as follows:
Canada has just completed a prosperous year and embarked on what appears to be another bright economic period.
He finds that production and employment were at record levels in 1959. He finds that recovery has continued relatively free of inflation, just as the Canadian Labour Congress finds that the inflation threat has been greatly exaggerated. Mr. Daniell goes on and adds this:
Economists and bankers generally agree that if costs and prices can continue to be maintained in the increasingly competitive world of international trade, the outlook is indeed rosy.
Let us take a look at the situation from the point of view of the municipalities. When the municipalities came to see the Prime Minister in November last, they had this to say:


The nation was never more prosperous than it is today. Nor is it because our cities and towns are impoverished. To the contrary, the productive wealth of the nation is highly concentrated in urban communities and is rising rapidly.
As one who has contributed his own share to deficit budgeting on the part of this government, let me say this: our municipal incentive program in the eyes of the opposition was contributory to deficit budgeting. This is the program which provided 40,000 jobs last winter and, as of now, the figure is in the neighbourhood of 34,000 for this winter. Since the program got started considerably earlier this year and this has been in answer to the requests of the various municipalities across Canada and the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities-the present figure is considerably above what it was at this time last year. The municipalities seem to like this program because they were back with a request for more of the same. This is what hon. members in the opposition call deficit budgeting. As a result of this deficit budgeting-and again I would refer hon. members to the Canadian Labour Congress brief-181,000 more Canadians are at work this winter than was the case last year. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what they think of deficit budgeting. I know what the Canadian Labour Congress thinks of it. They think it is all right.
Let us talk a little more of deficit budgeting; $750 million for homes; more than 280,000 homes built in 1958 and 1959. This is more deficit budgeting: in unemployment insurance more than $400 million paid out at the height of the recession. This I maintain, Mr. Speaker, placed purchasing power in the hands of Canadians who otherwise might have been destitute, who otherwise would have suffered. Does the hon. member for Essex East, or anyone in the opposition, think for one minute that he is the only person concerned with unemployment in this country? May I say this, Mr. Speaker. He only discovered unemployment in 1958 when he was in the opposition. Where was he in 1955 when unemployment was 6.8 per cent of the labour force, higher than it is today?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What figure is the minister taking when he mentions 6.8 per cent?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Dominion bureau of statistics. He was then known as silent Paul. He sat in his seat on the treasury benches saying nothing. Now he is Paul the pessimist. In 1955, when the jobless figure was 6.8 per cent of the labour force, how did they recognize unemployment?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Will the minister permit a question? Is this 6.8 per cent figure that the

minister is talking about for 1955 as the official figure the figure that the government takes now for unemployment in this country?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is correct; 6.8 per cent of the labour force, according to the D.B.S. official figures.
In the throne speech of that year this is how they recognized unemployment. They spoke of it in this way, and I quote:
Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature.
Then they postponed the unemployment debate for two weeks. That is how important that was. The then minister of labour said that unemployment must be considered "in a calm and dispassionate manner".
The minister of trade and commerce of that day said the N.E.S. figure did not represent true unemployment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is what you say now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What did the then minister of national health and welfare, now the hon. member for Essex East, say? Nothing. Unemployment is not new in this country. It has been growing steadily in cyclical movements since the end of the war. The cycle which started in 1946 was in full swing when we took office. Last winter was the high point of the trend. They did nothing about it. I say this: we have reversed that trend. They knew what the trend was all about in all of those years; they had their reports but they did nothing about the warnings they had. We took measures and reversed that trend. Instead of going up this winter, as they expected, the figure has settled back, so that our last D.B.S. figure was 70,000 below last winter.
Let us take a look at that picture. The D.B.S. figure is the official figure. I know the hon. member for Essex East will not take my word for it, but perhaps he will take the word of his former colleagues, the then minister of labour and the then minister of trade and commerce. When the then minister of trade and commerce told the Canadian people in this house at the height of unemployment in 1955 that the N.E.S. did not represent true unemployment I wonder whether he was kidding the Canadian people? If he was, why did the then minister of national health and welfare not rise in his place and let the Canadian people in on the secret? At every opportunity Mr. Howe, the then minister of trade and commerce, emphasized that the D.B.S. figure was the only measure of unemployment. Now, let us see what he said about the N.E.S. figure, that is, the national employment service registration figure, in February, 1954, and I quote from Hansard of that date at page 2103:
It is true that since about the middle of January this figure has exceeded half a million. However, 79951-0-33
The Address-Mr. Starr it should be made absolutely clear that this figure does not constitute the number of unemployed. As my colleague the Minister of Labour has pointed out to this house, this is simply a figure which becomes available through the operation of the employment service in carrying out its task of helping to place people in jobs. As such, the figure includes people who after registration find jobs on their own while failing to notify the employment office, and also people who-are working parttime but can qualify for benefits under the unemployment insurance regulations.
In June, 1954, Mr. Howe said this, as found on page 6123 of Hansard:
We have a situation where people register for jobs while they are employed. We also have a situation where a man will retire from the railroad on a pension and then put himself down as seeking a job. Would you list him as unemployed? The bureau of statistics would refer to him as a man outside the labour force. He had retired. Nevertheless, the labour department would include his name as an applicant for a job.
Talking about the bureau of statistics figure in 1955, Mr. Howe said this, as found on page 1629 of Hansard:
The labour force survey, which is the one set of statistics available giving a comprehensive and detailed description of Canada's labour force, sets the number of persons without jobs and seeking work at 362,000 this January, compared with 280,000 at the same date last year-
Now, let us hear from the former minister of labour, my predecessor. These words are found on page 1610 of Hansard for 1955:
-the 570,000 that my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago is not a static figure. It does not represent the same people from day to day, week to week or month to month. It is an ever-recurring figure of the number of workers who are often on short time unemployment.
Hansard does not record any objections at all by the hon. member for Essex East to these definitions-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It records a lot of definitions from your side though.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -by his respected colleagues. There has been a lot of talk about inflation, Mr. Speaker, and I ask your indulgence when I say that the inflation I have been most conscious of has been in the manner in which the hon. member for Essex East has mishandled these figures. What has been the picture in the last 12 months? Compared with the same figures for 1958, the D.B.S. figure has been consistently below last year's figures month by month since last February. Here are the figures, Mr. Speaker. In January of 1959 there was an increase of 11,000 over 1958. In February there was a decrease of 26,000 from the previous year. All these figures I am going to recite are comparable with 1958. In March, 1959, the figure was down 72,000, in April down 77,000, in May down 36,000, in June down 90,000, in July down 63,000, in August down 42,000, in
The Address-Mr. Starr September down 58,000, in October down 76,000, in November down 65,000 and in December down 70,000, which is the last figure available from the bureau of statistics.
There are still thousands of unemployed.

What about the voices of doom and the prophecies of disaster? We halted the rising trend that had been manifest since the war. This was the year of the roll-back in the rising trend in unemployment, a trend that the opposition knew about, said nothing about and did nothing about.
Let us take a look at this trend. It began in 1946. There were peaks and valleys but the trend was always upward. In 1954,
6.1	per cent of the labour force was unemployed and in 1955, 7.4 per cent. In 1955 the then minister of trade and commerce pointed out the difficulties and said, as found on page 1630 of Hansard:
This levelling off in productive activity was the result of certain new influences which began to affect the market situation in the latter part of 1953 and early 1954. Hon. members are no doubt aware of most of the difficulties encountered-a general business let-down in the United States: a consequent decline during 1954 in Canadian exports to that market; reduced incomes of grain producers, and the effects of this on sales of farm equipment and other manufactured goods-a tendency during 1954 for businesses to meet orders from inventories rather than new production; and, finally, intensification of international competition in manufactured goods which presented new difficulties-
All these factors were present in intensified form when we took office 18 months later. They had done nothing about them. What did we do about the situation? Anyone who wants to know what we did about declining exports to the United States had better take a good look at last year's figures. What did we do about lessened markets for grain producers? From August to December last year overseas wheat sales were up 10.3 per cent. They said it could not be done but we did it. They even went out west and told the farmers it could not be done but the farmers did not believe them and the farmers were right.
These same farmers I am talking about bought 25 per cent more farm equipment and farm machinery this year than last year. Last week when we brought in a bill to assist these same farmers what did they do? They said they liked the idea but they did not approve of the way it was being done. It is the same old story. The old policy was "do nothing", and the new policy is "stop everything".
Last week the hon. member for Essex East discovered, through information which I had given him, that some 722,834 persons were registered with the unemployment

insurance commission. What does that figure represent? In the first place it represents more than 166,000 women.
What is wrong with that?

I am coming to the point, if the hon. member will give me the opportunity. The house will recall that we relaxed the restrictions on married women imposed by the previous government. We did that in the year 1957. We followed no double standard in our legislation. We placed working wives and mothers on the same basis as married men.
This figure of 722,834 also represented 110,000 unskilled construction workers, the very nature of whose work is seasonal. It represents more than 8,000 construction machine operators, whose work is seasonal. It represents more than 18,000 loggers and bushworkers, whose work is seasonal. I may say that 3,000 more men are employed in the bush this year than last year. The figure represents more than 40,000 persons registered as carpenters across Canada, whose work is subject to seasonal falling off.
This seasonality in the construction and building industries is one of the things my department has been fighting with our intensified winter work campaign which in the last two years has brought startling changes in the construction industry in Canada. The figure, as Mr. Howe pointed out in 1954, represents a large number of persons with pensions. It includes a number of persons with jobs registering for other jobs. It includes nearly 10,000 workers in the tobacco industry, whose work is subject to seasonal factors. It includes 7,200 bricklayers. It includes 12,000 persons registered as painters. All of these are seasonal workers. It also includes stevedores on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river and longshoremen on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river who, we all know, are seasonal workers.
When you get into the skilled worker groups you find that the number of registrations is much smaller. The reason is that our economy is producing a greater and greater demand for skilled workers. In cooperation with the provinces we are moving to increase the level of skills by setting up standards for apprentices across Canada and by encouraging the fullest use of the vocational training program. We co-operate with the provinces on a 50-50 basis. We are urging them at all times-and I personally wrote to the provinces-to make the fullest use of this plan. I may say that training is being provided at an increased rate for unemployed persons in courses approved by the unemployment insurance commission. Those approved courses number well over 500. We

are now moving to include more and more of those courses so that these people while in training are able to draw unemployment insurance providing they have the necessary contributions.
Will the minister allow a question?
Yes.
What is the minister's estimate of the actual number of unemployed under the I.L.O.?

The D.B.S. figure is recognized by the I.L.O. The standard has been set by the I.L.O. and has also been followed by the United States labour department. We are carrying on with the same figure. The figure that was recognized by the former government. I refer of course to the D.B.S. figure. The last D.B.S. release was for mid-December and it showed 370,000.
Combined?
Combined; that is right; that includes men and women.
Will the minister permit another question in order to clarify the situation?

I have only 40 minutes at my disposal. If hon. members would wait to ask their questions until I am finished I shall be glad to answer any questions I am able to answer.
I have said that training is being taken at an increased rate by unemployed persons in courses approved by the unemployment insurance commission. We hope to bring in more of these courses. We have recently expanded the number of approved courses also so that the number of unemployed persons to receive such training in the coming year should be considerably greater than was this year's figure of 5,000. I am not satisfied. Five thousand is not enough. I think we should be retraining as many as require retraining and that is our goal.
We are also conducting surveys on the effects of automation, so that measures can be evolved to minimize the dislocation caused by the advance of technology.
The house will also recall that I have repeatedly stressed the importance of job placements in the unemployment insurance operation. That was one of the first things that I tried to do. The placements in the month of December just past were 74,801, the highest since 1944. I quote from a report of the unemployment insurance commission. This is what it says:
While higher placements were to be expected in 1959 as compared with 1957 and 1958 because of improving economic conditions, much of the 79951-0-33J
The Address-Mr. Starr
1959 achievement results from improved employment service operations under the stimulus of the re-emphasis program.
I am very happy to report that.
I have spoken about the rising unemployment cycle under the previous administration and I have cited the testimony of the former minister of trade and commerce with regard to the situation in 1955. I would ask the house to examine with me the unemployment figures during the years when the present opposition were in office and when this cycle was developing. We find that in 1946 the figure for unemployment was 4.7 of the labour force.
Is that a D.B.S. figure?
I am quoting only D.B.S. figures.
I was just asking.

These are all D.B.S. figures. In 1947 the figure was 3 per cent; in 1948,
3.2	per cent; in 1949, 4 per cent; in 1950, 6.1 per cent. That was the first cycle. Korea got them off the hook. In 1951 the figure was back down to 3.3 per cent. In 1952 the figure went back up to 4 per cent. In 1953 it was 3.4 per cent. In 1954 it was 6 per cent in February and 7 per cent in March. The second cycle was in full swing again. In 1955 it was 7.4 per cent in March. Hon. members opposite still had not discovered unemployment. There is no evidence that they recognized this trend and did anything about it. In 1956 they had taken no action and unemployment went down to 5.5 per cent and up to 5.6 per cent in 1957. Once again there was that rise moving into the next cycle as their economists predicted it would. In 1958 it was 9.4 per cent.
Tory times, hard times.

I am giving you figures during your time too. Therefore you can see what the trend had been since 1946. In early 1959 it levelled off to 8.8 per cent. The figure in December, 1959 is 5.9 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I have given the whole trend. I have taken it step by step since 1946. You can see what happened up to 1951. Korea got them off the hook. The situation reversed in 1956. The measures we took when we saw the situation reversed that trend and we have the evidence now. This was recognized in the brief submitted yesterday by the Canadian Labour Congress. The former government had the figures. They had the reports showing the trend. They had those confidential reports that showed these trends but they never let the people in on the secret. They sat it out; and one of the greatest sitter-outers was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). You never heard a peep out of him about unemployment in 1955.

The Address-Mr. Starr
In 1958 he discovered unemployment and that discovery was accompanied by a great display of drama here in this house. Like the famous general, he went galloping off in all directions, scattering warnings of doom and depression. Last session one speech during the throne speech debate was not enough for the hon. member for Essex East. He had to make another appearance. The first appearance he made was on January 22 and like the prophet of old, he was back again on January 30. The disaster warnings grew thick and fast during both of these appearances.
In his second appearance he warned the government that its policies were not meeting the approval of the bank presidents and big corporation directors of this country. He showed the same solicitude in the industrial relations committee last year when we had the unemployment insurance amendments before that committee and when he demanded that the unemployment insurance fund be replenished from general tax revenues. What does that mean? This would have had the effect of relieving the corporations from paying increased contributions. He did that with the unemployment insurance amendments that he piloted through this house. On that occasion, he was acting on behalf of the then minister of labour. Where were the increases? Were the increases in the employer contributions? No, Mr. Speaker; the record shows clearly and plainly-and I set it out here last session-that during the committee stage on the bill the hon. member for Essex East levied all the increases on contributions from the employees.
If we had followed his suggestion in supplying these increased contributions from general tax revenues, replenishing the fund from general tax revenues it would have meant higher taxes for ordinary Canadians. Now, what is the employment situation today? The D.B.S. figure-the figure that the former government said was the only true figure for unemployment-was 370,000 in December. It was only 8,000 more than in January 1955, when there was not one peep from the hon. member for Essex East. The December figure represents 5.9 per cent of the labour forces; at the same time last year the figure was 7.2 per cent of the labour forces.
When the Prime Minister spoke in the early part of the throne speech debate he quoted some remarks made by the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce as follows:
In September, less than 3 per cent of the labour iorce was unemployed, which, allowing for temporary unemployment and the unemployable, is considered to be full employment.

If 3 per cent in September, was full employment, 5.9 per cent in December, allowing for seasonal factors, is not too bad. The figure in the United States for December is 5.2 per cent, and in the United States they are getting the full benefit of the back to work movement resulting from the steel strike settlement, which we do not get in this country until a full month later.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. minister, but I must inform him that his time has expired.
Carry on.
Mr. Speaker, this is an important discussion, and on behalf of all hon. members I ask that the minister be allowed to proceed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the house give unanimous consent that the minister be allowed to finish his speech?
Agreed.
I do not agree with the minister's statement, but I agree that he should continue.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members for allowing me to carry on. I might say to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) that he has the right to disagree with me, but I want to point out to him that the figures I am quoting here are correct and these are the facts.
All I am saying is that the minister continues. We want to hear what he has to say about labour.

A lot has been said about tight money, and I want to deal with that briefly because my department deals with jobs, not money. The Leader of the Opposition in his opening speech criticised the Prime Minister for making a plea on behalf of the small borrower. They did not know in 1955 that the small borrower existed. When you look at the bank statements, the Prime Minister's words were not without effect. They had been made aware of his concern for these people.
In the statement of the president of a national Canadian bank the following appears:
In their allocation of their available resources between the various categories of customers, the chartered banks gave special consideration to the small borrower, as witnessed by the following figures issued by the Canadian banker's association-
Then Mr. Roberge goes on to give the figures. Mr. Muir, president of the Royal

Bank, after paying tribute to the wisdom and courage of those in charge of fiscal policy, goes on to say:
The savings of the general public who bought the bonds were channelled into new loans to businessmen, farmers and consumers. There was no creation of new money, only the channelling of savings into loans through the mobilization by the banks of the existing money supply. Idle capacity and idle men were thus put to work and production was thereby maintained or increased with no undue build up of inflationary pressures.
The banks were thus very conscious of the small borrower, in great contrast to 1955 when they left the small borrower right out of the picture.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the situation in 1955 was very different. As Mr. Howe pointed out, there was a declining economy: trade was down; inventories were up. It was just at this time that they brought in tight money. They brought it in as a matter of deliberate, positive government policy and, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out the other night, they controlled the banks.
Now; under the circumstances, it was the worst possible move they could have made. Never has there been a more striking example of blundering and confusion in government policy. As the Prime Minister pointed out the other day, the situation in the last year was entirely different. The economy was on the rise. In the words of the Canadian Labour Congress, employment was up, unemployment was down. A terrific expansion was in effect. The demand for credit simply outstripped the available supply. In 1955 you had the banks rebelling against government policy which was strangling their operations. This year you have commendation for fiscal policy.
Mr. Speaker, the dispensation we granted the hon. minister was, I thought, on the understanding that we were going to hear government policy. Is that going to occur?
I am sorry; I did not hear the question.
When the time limit was reached the minister said, as I understood it, he was going to give us the labour policy, not make a government speech.

As Minister of Labour I feel I should enlighten the house and particularly those who are in a state of confusion, and put before them the correct situation with regard to unemployment and the economy instead of putting forward various figures for political purposes.
What about the recession? Everybody knows that the recession is over. Everybody, that is, except those hon. members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Essex East
The Address-Mr. Starr and his group. I think they should form a doomsters union. Wherever you look the picture is the same. Department store sales are 6.1 per cent ahead of last year. Chain stores are up 6.2 per cent. Let us look at the automobile industry, and I have mentioned what is happening in the city of Oshawa, in the riding I represent. Production in the automobile industry in Canada is up 26.4 per cent over last year. Production at January 16 this year was up 24.4 per cent over last month. Now, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is that recession?
Industrial production in general is up by 11 per cent. Newsprint is up 8 per cent. Mineral production is up 19 per cent. Labour income is up 9.3 per cent.
Taxes are up, too.
The hon. member talks about taxes. Taxes are lower now than they were before June 1957.
Oh, oh.

I can well understand the frustration of hon. members opposite. They do not like this picture which shows that there is buoyancy in our economy and that we are out of the recession that they knew something about but did nothing about. That is quite understandable.
As I say, labour income is up 9.3 per cent. The evidence is overwhelming wherever you look.
How is the birth rate doing?
Babies like being born under a Conservative government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must ask hon. members to allow the minister to continue his remarks.

Now, what does this prove? It proves that the measures taken by this government have played an important part in stemming the tide of recession and restoring the forward movement of the economy, and this is acknowledged by the Canadian Labour Congress in the brief they presented yesterday. As we move into 1960 there is confidence and optimism in the minds of most people in this country. With one exception. In the front benches opposite, doom and depression continue their dreary reign. We leave them to their doom and gloom, Mr. Speaker. It is said that prophets have no honour in their own country. In this country the prophets of doom and despair have been proven abundantly wrong, and if there is no honour it is a situation of their own making.
As Minister of Labour I want to say this in conclusion: that ever since I assumed this office I have endeavoured to do all I can to better the lives and conditions of Canadians.

The Address-Mr. Tardif I will continue to do so. The wishes and the desires of working men and women in this country will always receive my consideration and my personal attention.

May I ask the minister a question? Will the minister confirm that almost 100 per cent of the claimants for unemployment insurance benefits who are registered at unemployment insurance offices are actually out of work, and that benefits would not be paid to them unless they were recognized as unemployed.

I spent a considerable amount of time quoting figures with respect to those people who were registered in the categories which the hon. member mentions, and I leave him to judge the extent of unemployment with regard to the nature of the work and the seasonal aspect of the undertakings.
Another question: would unemployment insurance benefits be paid to them if they were not unemployed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister was given unanimous consent to continue his remarks, but if there is to be a period of questioning I think further consent of the house is necessary-
The minister has agreed to answer.

speechtext: To answer some questions, but I think we are starting on a series of questions.
Closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no closure, may I remind the hon. member for Gloucester. I do not think that word should be used.
It was I who moved that the minister should be given time to continue his speech, but what I expected was not a review of the past but an explanation of how he, in his policy-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We gave unanimous consent that the minister should continue his remarks, but not to say what the hon. member for Vancouver East expected him to say or wanted him to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have recognized the hon. member for Russell, (Mr. Tardif).
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, even with my short experience, I can see that it is traditional to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It affords

me great pleasure therefore to congratulate the hon. members for Rimouski and Gren-ville-Dundas (Mr. Morissette and Mrs.. Cas-selman) who performed their task like professionals. The hon. member for Gren-ville-Dundas (Mr. Morissette and Mrs. Cas-which is the envy of all members of the house.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the warm welcome you extended to me when I was introduced to this house.
In fact, it was with a certain feeling of humility that I took my place in this house. With assistance from my colleagues, I intend to do my utmost to provide the citizens of beautiful Russell county and Canadians as a whole with the kind of government they deserve.
I want to take this opportunity of congratulating the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Flynn), who, I am sure, will discharge his responsibilities with his well known dignity and fairness.
Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I did not tender my best wishes to the parliamentary secretaries who have just been appointed for the period of one year.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Russell, which I have the honour to represent within the Liberal party, has considerably changed in the past few years, as have indeed various other parts of Canada. The constituency was known as a rural riding with very limited urban development. Today, it is mainly urban, though preserving its rural character. Its ever-increasing population comprises all Canadian elements. This part of the country has a great many farmers, businessmen, professional men, quite a few craftsmen and an impressive number of government employees.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to mention the warm welcome which I had from both sides of the house when I officially made my entry here. I already felt accepted by those who take an interest in the administration of this country.
I had then decided to postpone my maiden speech to the house, in order to have time to learn the procedure and watch the government at work. I now realize that it will not be necessary, and that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not take the floor now.
In fact, one of the election promises-and there were not many of them-which I made to the electors of the constituency of Russell, was that I would not be a silent representative, especially when their interests, or those of Canadians as a whole, would be at stake.
(Text):
I know you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to express my reaction to the speech from the throne as it was presented to this house a

few days ago. I am referring to the official one, not the unofficial one by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on January 15. That, I feel, was made for political propaganda purposes. My reaction to the speech from the throne was twofold. Speaking for myself and adopting a selfish attitude, I could say what I told the electors of Russell during my campaign-that the speech from the throne would be famous not for what it contained but for what it omitted. I told the voters at that time that it would be evident that none of the problems which affect Canada at this time would be reflected in the speech from the throne and that no solution to any of our pressing problems would be offered.
I am afraid-and this is the opinion of other Canadians after reading the speech from the throne-that there is an evident lack of policy and a definite lack of solutions to many of the present problems which affect every one of those in my constituency.
Today, with the exception of the speech to which I just listened made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr)-and I must accuse myself of lack of experience because I found it most confusing-no reference was made to the present tight money policy or any proposed action by the government to alleviate the painful results of such policy or lack of policy.
I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would probably hasten to say that no such policy exists. I am now referring to a tight money policy. I know they would maintain the attitude of saying nothing about it as has been the practice. I know that the Minister of Finance would probably state as he did in Toronto in the speech he made to the board of trade that the effects can be countered only by hard work, privation and a general lowering of the standard of living. That is certainly the effect it has on the ordinary citizen on the street. I am particularly worried about the effects of tight money on the segment of the population in my riding and on all Canadians.
I cannot resist the temptation of reading a statement made by the Minister of Finance on January 27, 1958, as reported at page 3852 of Hansard of that date:
The municipalities, particularly, have been hampered and restrained by high costs and difficulties of borrowing in recent years, and on them has fallen much of the burden of the tight money policy which has been prevailing in the past several years.
The minister at that time was referring to the Liberal government. He continued:
That tight money policy has now been eased in line with the policies of this government-
The Address-Mr. Tardif
The hon. gentleman went on to explain that he and his government intended to do something about it. The effects of what he intended to do are not evident as far as I am personally concerned. Mr. Robert Duffy, a famous columnist in the Globe and Mail, in an article on August 27, 1959 observed:
Meanwhile we have the government's efforts to explain when and how the tight money policy is not a tight money policy.
The short answer for the time being seems to be: When a Conservative government is in power.
Mr. Blair Fraser who is a recognized authority on financial questions and a famous writer in an article dated September 26, 1958, stated:
Seldom have reporters been baffled as they were when Prime Minister Diefenbaker, back from the west, undertook to explain about tight money.
What he said was clear: "There is no tight money policy. There was one three years ago. but there isn't now." Just what did he mean? What exactly did we have three years ago we haven't got now?
There have been so many utterances made by the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance that could be quoted. However, I am going to reserve some of my ammunition for the future in the event there is a general election in the near future.
I am personally thinking of the extra cost that tight money will bring to the farming community the members of which have to buy or replace machinery and equipment at terms bearing a high rate of interest. I am thinking of the small rural school board that will have to secure facilities for a growing child population and will be saddled by exorbitant interest payments on debentures they will have a great deal of difficulty to market and will continue to be penalized for 20 or 25 years with a high rate of interest that will be set when they do the borrowing. This will become our children's inherited mortgage as it was described by President Eisenhower in his state of the union message. This applies to small business and small industries and eventually will reflect on the standard of living of the artisans, many of them being seasonal workers.
No reference was made in the speech from the throne to a policy concerning national defence. While every Canadian is desirous of maintaining permanent peace he is also aware of the importance of being properly prepared for defending his country. The man on the street is worried at not having heard any program of defence in the speech from the throne and at the lack of such policies.
No reference was made in the throne speech to unemployment. A few days ago the Minister of Labour stated to the house that as of December 31 last there were approximately 700,000 Canadians unemployed. At the risk

The Address-Mr. Tardif of exposing myself to accusations of being repetitious I must say this brings to mind the declaration made by the Prime Minister.
It should be brought to mind.

of fear in the minds of civil servants. The lack of action on the part of the government to take any step to rectify the present condition is a very bad example to all other employers in Canada.
Much can be said of the lack of a program to improve the lot of small farmers, of milk producers and of cheese makers. Nothing was said with regard to what should have been a promise on the part of the government to submit a program to this house that would allow the small farmer to expect and receive a scale of income that would be commensurate with the income paid to trained workers. The eastern farmers have no objection to, as a matter of fact they support most heartily, the action taken by this house to help the western farmer in the calamity that has befallen him. However, they had hoped that the government would have introduced legislation to look after the needs of the eastern farmers who may find themselves in trouble should a similar situation occur in the eastern part of Canada. However, a lot of these things can be taken up when the estimates are before the house.
We have not had a word from the government in connection with the national capital, not a word to assure the people of the Canadian capital that more will be done by the government to accelerate the development of our wonderful national capital. With the exception of the declaration by the Prime Minister on January 25 when he said that the liaison established between the N.C.C. and the Prime Minister of Canada was now to be transferred to the Department of Public Works-which I suspect was done for political reasons-there was not a word referring to the injustices in the purchase of land in the green belt area where the price paid by the federal government for expropriated land is much below the price paid by private enterprise for land abutting the designated green belt area.
There was no mention by the government of its intention of retaining in the city of Ottawa and in the surrounding areas the public buildings that are necessary for the administration of this country. There was not a word in the speech from the throne of the government's intentions of making known to the province of Quebec and the city of Ottawa the percentage that it is ready and willing to contribute to the much needed interprovincial bridge between the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull. However, Mr. Barrette, the new premier of the province of Quebec, stated, and I quote from he Droit of January 20, 1960:
Prime Minister Antonio Barrette stated on Tuesday to a delegation of the chamber of commerce of the province that the government of Quebec
The Address-Mr. Tardif was well disposed and ready to do its part for the construction of a bridge between Hull and Ottawa, but that the initiative must come from the federal authorities.
There is an election coming in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me I should like to draw to the attention of the house some of my experiences in the Russell by-election. I feel quite sure that you will find them interesting. In the first place, may I quote from the Citizen of October 3, 1959. I refer to an editorial entitled:
The Issues in Russell.
I am not going to read the whole editorial but only a few parts of it. I shall save the rest of it until the ministers are all in their places.
After only two years in office, the Conservatives have revealed a singular bankruptcy of ideas- perhaps because, in the first instance, they had no real ideas, but only a program based on political opportunism. In any event, they have nothing to oiler Russell voters except an appeal to climb on the bandwagon.
A little farther down we find this:
The bandwagon is already overloaded with members from more than 200 constituencies, most of whom have little more voice in the nation's affairs than the voters they represent.
I think this is an excellent editorial, Mr. Speaker. I will forego the pleasure of reading it all and save it for another occasion.
I know you will find it in order for me to give a few details concerning the Russell by-election. Remarks were made at one time or another, as is always the case, during the campaign that preceded the election of October 5 in the riding of Russell. I have to accuse myself of being guilty at that time of an excessive amount of pride. I noted the activities on the part of the government to add one more seat to the government, one more backbenchers' backbencher. I am referring to that number of bold, silent men who sit in the back rows on the government side. All this I thought was done because of the government's fear of my personal power.
This sin was soon regretted and it was atoned for when it was evident that the whole Russell election strategy was for the purpose of adding another rose to the Prime Minister's already overcrowded crown, a crown that he probably finds difficult to carry at times. The campaign was the brain child of the chief organizer of the Conservative party who is a genius of organization according to his own estimation. The program evidently was to make Russell riding by-election a miniature general election. This was done, Mr. Speaker, complete with slogans similar to those used to sell soap.

The Address-Mr. Tardif
I was surprised and flattered by the great number of ministers of the crown and their charming wives who took a very active part in the Russell by-election. I understand there were enough ministers in Russell at that time to have a cabinet meeting and I expect that a cabinet meeting was probably held. We did not hear about it because it oftens happens that cabinet meetings are held, nothing comes from them and nothing is accomplished.
This was not all. The election campaign in Russell was not a defence in depth but an all-out offensive, with the ordinary workers making up the army, the ordinary Union Nationale-trained Conservative members from Quebec being the officer corps and the members of the federal cabinet being the big guns, eight in all.
Name them.

If time permits I will be very glad to name them. The Prime Minister, according to tradition, did not mix in the Russell by-election in a manner that was evident but he did make a junket around the riding for the purpose of shaking hands and in the adjoining municipalities and, indeed, the municipalities of the province of Quebec. He ended all this with a television broadcast to the nation four days before the election, giving the election a flavour of a three-ringed circus.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, they came, bully boys and all, and spare voters too. The chief Tory organizer had given the word. There was to be no mention of policy during the campaign. The theme was, give Dief a vote of confidence, make him feel happy. The interpretation given to all this by the Liberal candidate was, give Dief an additional backbencher who, like a great number of the members supporting the government, will never be heard.
What about the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell)?

The hon. member for Carleton was also there but I had no objection to that and was not offended. The reasons I have enumerated are the reasons for my changing my original decision to wait until later to be heard in the house because it was one of my election promises that I would not be a backbencher from the point of view of action. I promised the people of Russell that I would make my voice heard and I have had the permission of all the Liberals in the house to do so on every occasion.
All this came to pass, Mr. Speaker. The people of Russell have again proven that those who see the present administration in action or in lack of action must of necessity vote against it, and they bravely did so in

an overwhelming manner. It is my intention and it will be my pleasant duty to contribute all the time I can to constructive, fearless opposition according to the policies set by my party for the greatest good of the people of Russell and the people of Canada generally.
If I have a few moments left at my disposal I should like to thank the members of the Conservative party who were so helpful in making my election campaign in Russell a success. They include the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough), the former secretary of state, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley), the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton). Incidentally, I also want to thank their wives for their contribution.
It would not be fair, Mr. Speaker, if I did not include the names of the private members who also made a contribution such as the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais), the hon. member for Riviere du Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Frechette), the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau), the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade), the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Monteith), the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Dubois), the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere), the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Rompre), the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Richard), the hon. member for Chateauguay-Hunting-don-Laprairie (Mr. Barrington), the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages), the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Grenier), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers), the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Latour), the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson), the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Bruchesi), the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. LaRue), the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Deschambault), the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Letour-neau), the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) and finally, as I learned today and must not forget, the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Campeau).

Mr. Speaker, I have just been listening to the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) who said in his first remarks that he entered this house with a certain sense of humility; however, after hearing his speech, it is obvious that his humility has changed into cocksureness.
However, my dear fellow member, having been in this house longer than you, let me tell you that if you keep making such statements in the house, you may have a surprise in your constituency at the next election.
Are you jealous? Are you jealous?
He will double his majority.
Did I get that right?

Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on your appointment as chairman of committees. The Prime Minister could not have made a better choice. I have known your great qualities for a long time, and I am sure your sound judgment will be an important factor in ensuring respect for our parliamentary institutions.
I also wish to congratulate the hon. members for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) and for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) for the confidence which the Prime Minister has shown them by taking them into the cabinet. I am sure their ability and sense of duty will adequately serve the interests of the nation.
I would be remiss in failing to mention the speeches of the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Morissette and Mrs. Casselman). The member for Rimouski, in his usual way, made a responsible and well balanced speech. He even took the economic experts of the opposition by surprise.
The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), with all her charm and dignity, spoke very ably of the problems of her constituency and also gave us her views on some international problems of great importance.
Recently, Mr. Speaker, newspapers in the province of Quebec made quite a fuss about the Quebec members silence on the moot question of winter navigation. Among other things, Conservative members were 79951-0-34J
The Address-Mr. Asselin taken to task for not bringing the appropriate pressure to bear upon this government so that the icebreakers could regularly convoy ships sailing up the St. Lawrence river to Quebec in the wintertime. The papers brought up the fancied idea of competition between Quebec harbour and the maritime provinces, indicating that our icebreakers are assigned to minor jobs.
I feel that those newspapers did not place the problem in its proper context and did not consider the economic and climatic conditions of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence.
I should like to make it clear that the ideas I am going to put to this house are not in any way binding on members of this government; they are merely the result of the experience of the member for the county of Charlevoix where year-round navigation has been practised for the last 30 years.
In 1957, Mr. Speaker, a large Quebec city organization convinced businessmen and shipping firms that winter navigation was feasible up to Quebec during the winter. The Federal Commercial Navigation Company offered its services for the tests by making available to Quebec harbour the D'Vora which was to carry goods from Quebec to the north shore.
Exceptional weather and ice conditions gave acceptable results during this first experiment, but it must be said that the crew ran into risks and perils which, on several occasions, endangered the passengers' lives.
In 1957, like today, the D'Vora was, from Pointe au Pic on, unable to sail up the river without the help of icebreakers. On several occasions, I saw the D'Vora come alongside the wharf at Pointe au Pic, and wait there several days for an icebreaker which was making its usual round on the river, and which would escort it up to Quebec.
After that first encouraging test, other ships were mustered in 1958 and 1959 to send goods from Quebec to the north shore-all this while still facing the same difficulties.
In 1959, some trans-Atlantic shipping companies, who had reinforced ships, equipped to resist the ice, were invited to sail up to Quebec; and I do not think that, when this second experiment was started, the government had given any assurance of making a scheduled icebreaker service available to vessels sailing up the river to Quebec during the winter.

The Address-Mr. Asselin
I may perhaps be accused of being opposed to winter navigation to Quebec. I shall immediately answer that I favour winter navigation, but I am also thinking of the economic factors on which such project should be based. I am also not siding with the maritimes against Quebec, but I say that winter navigation up to Quebec has unfairly competed with the winter harbour at Pointe au Pic, and it is my duty to protect that economic sector in my riding.
Everybody knows that for the last 30 years there has been year round navigation at Pointe au Pic. There is at that spot an atmospheric occurrence which, because of water currents and the direction of the winds, frees the river and the harbour of Pointe au Pic from ice so that ships may enter the harbour and depart again with their cargo without the help of icebreakers. During the last war, navy vessels were moored there on various occasions during their winter manoeuvres and, there again, they had no need of icebreakers.
To give only a few figures, the Clarke Steamship Company Limited carried during the winter of 1956-1957, up to 1,500 tons of goods from Pointe au Pic to the north shore. Such activity in the harbour of Pointe au Pic gave work to about a hundred longshoremen, and our heads of families could thus benefit from a substantial income, since the Clarke Steamship Limited paid, in a single winter season, from $45,000 to $50,000 in wages.
This year, winter navigation up to Quebec has practically brought economic activity to a standstill at Pointe au Pic. This year, as at January 6, 1960, about $1,200 had been paid in wages, and only one shipment of 60 tons was loaded, while at one time Pointe au Pic and Rimouski were considered the only winter harbours in eastern Quebec. Today, those two winter harbours are used only as second-rate harbours, and in case of extreme necessity. The one at Pointe au Pic is now used only as a shelter for ships in difficulty or threatened by ice on the St. Lawrence.
Thus, competition is being met in an economic sector of the same province. This year at Pointe au Pic the Department of Public Works built a wharf extension, as well as a vast and highly modern shed, at the cost of nearly $750,000, to help steamship companies that operate in the wintertime; but now those improvements are useless, because,

to all appearances, Quebec is becoming the sole harbour for wintertime shipping.
Last year, the Canadian National Railway authorities granted the Charlevoix area a preferential rate on the rail transport of goods to Pointe au Pic, so as to help those companies enjoy reasonable rates of transport on the goods they ship to Pointe au Pic. Immediately there were loud protests from the city of Quebec about the Canadian National decision.
I wonder whether this attitude looks anything like true and loyal competition.
At present the harbour of Quebec is competing with the Canadian National Railways which operates between Quebec and La Malbaie. That public service has been operating at a loss for years, and it could reduce its deficit when rail shipments from Quebec to Pointe au Pic were normal. Freight trains which had been routed to Pointe au Pic have been stopped at Quebec because shippers were given to understand that the harbour at Quebec was the only one able to handle goods for shipment on the north shore. This action of course has meant the loss of thousands of dollars to people in my constituency, because the harbour at Pointe au Pic remained almost idle ever since Quebec officials managed to convince shipping companies that winter navigation was normal between Quebec and the north shore.
However, I happen to know that loaded ships have remained moored for weeks on end in Quebec harbour, unable as they were because of weather and ice conditions to risk sailing down the St. Lawrence. This necessarily entailed considerable delay in the delivery of goods to north shore people, and high storage costs. It was, too, unfair to Pointe au Pic harbour which is always ice-free and, for that reason allows ships to take on cargo with no delays due to any physical or atmospheric factor.
These last few days, Mr. Speaker, the matter of winter shipping has aroused interest not only in Quebec city but in other centres like Three Rivers and Montreal. I am informed that the chamber of commerce of Three Rivers has made representations to get regular icebreaker services so that the harbour of Three Rivers can benefit from winter navigation. Last week, the Ottawa Citizen and Le Devoir of Montreal put forward the idea that winter navigation would be possible up to Montreal provided of course that the

federal government would make additional icebreakers available to the Montreal harbour authorities. To support those claims, it is argued that if winter navigation is possible up to Quebec, there is no reason why it should not be so up to Three Rivers and even to Montreal. Now we are faced with a problem more complicated than was at first expected.
In order to make an objective study of the situation, I believe that we should first focus the discussion on the physical, atmospheric and economic aspects.
It has been established-as I said at the beginning of my speech-that winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river above Pointe au Pic, seems dangerous and almost impracticable because of the considerable amount of ice across this narrow neck of the St. Lawrence river, unless ships are well enough protected and equipped to withstand ice pressure. It is only when the weather is perfect and exceptionally good that ships can sail that distance up to Quebec, but not without facing imminent risks, unless they can depend on the scheduled aid of icebreakers; and even then, there are still certain risks and dangers.
My impression is that the experience already made on winter navigation up to Quebec should have started first, with a complete study of all factors and obstacles related to that question.
I would even add that such a study could not be made on a unilateral basis but had to be done in co-operation with the Department of Transport, because of the need to know in advance what help the department might provide for such an undertaking.
The Quebec port authorities launched this project without making a thorough study of the question. And now that difficulties have come up, the government is blamed for failing to provide assistance for the project, as desired by its promoters.
The member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), who never misses an opportunity to make political hay, has just joined in the debate with regard to this matter of winter navigation. Yet God knows that in the 18 years he has been sitting on the Liberal side as a private member and as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works, he had many opportunities to act on this project. But no, Mr. Speaker, in all that time, he never said a word. Now
The Address-Mr. Asselin he attempts to take credit away from the member for Quebec East (Mr. Tasse) who is the promoter of this project. Last Tuesday, January 26, 1960, he attempted-quite skillfully I admit-to show a contradiction between the statements of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and those of the member for Quebec East concerning icebreaker services which were to be provided on the St. Lawrence river. He tried to raise a doubt, but without committing himself. He was afraid to take a clear-cut position. He prefers to wait and see which way the wind blows, and find out what side would be more profitable from an election point of view. If he is so brave and he speaks for the Liberal party in the matter of winter navigation to Quebec, let him come out and tell us whether he is for or against such a thing.
The hon. member for Laurier and former minister of transport (Mr. Chevrier), who never gave a thought to this matter when he was in office, questioned the present Minister of Transport the other day in the house on the provision of regular icebreaker services in wintertime for ships sailing up the St. Lawrence to Quebec. The Minister of Transport replied that his department was giving maximum assistance at the present time. In saying he was giving maximum aid, I presume the Minister of Transport meant he was concerned with the problem and that his department so far had been giving maximum help, consistent with winter shipping regulations, to ships in need of icebreaker services.
I know quite well that last Christmas eve, the Swedish ship Elga Dan, sailing towards Quebec, had trouble on the river because of ice conditions. The icebreaker d'Iberville was called, and helped the ship break free and resume its course.
And the Liberal party will have the people of the province of Quebec believe that the winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river is of no concern to the Department of Transport.
I remember that on January 19, 1960, in this house, the hon. member for Levis pointed out to the Minister of Transport that if there were not enough icebreakers, there were shipyards in Lauzon, implying that the Department of Transport could have some built there.
I think this is the crux of the whole matter.
Did anyone figure the cost of operating an icebreaker, the cost of building additional

The Address-Mr. Asselin icebreakers and the number required to ensure ocean shipping in wintertime up to Quebec city?
Have the supporters of winter navigation up to Quebec city asked themselves the following questions?
How many icebreakers would be needed to ensure navigation for all ships that wish to sail up to Quebec? And then, when reaching Quebec how many icebreakers more would be needed to go to Three Rivers and to Montreal? How could the expense in capital and operation costs be compared with the profits this would bring to the harbours of Quebec, Three Rivers and Montreal, taking into account the losses which will be sustained by the St. Lawrence harbours operating all the year round at a small cost, as well as the loss of revenue for the harbours of Pointe au Pic, of Rimouski, of the Saguenay, *

not forgetting those of the Canadian National Railways? Is it possible to claim now, on the grounds of persecution, that the government should incur considerable expense in building additional icebreakers without first insuring that the undertaking will be at least self-supporting, when specialists in this field have already maintained that winter navigation pays its way in the harbours of Rimouski and Pointe au Pic?
All those considerations lead me to suggest that the government should seriously consider the winter navigation situation on the St. Lawrence and take positive action, in keeping with the conclusions of that survey.
I commend the government for its wise policy in solving that problem.
Elementary logic demands that the government should not commit itself to exorbitant expenses to ensure regular escort, in winter time, for ships wishing to sail up the St. Lawrence as far as Quebec, or farther, unless it has satisfactory evidence that such an undertaking is economically self-supporting.
In my opinion, it would be more efficient for fervent supporters of winter navigation to consider the problem from that angle in the first place before having people believe that the government is unconcerned, when in fact it has been giving the matter continuous and serious consideration in relation to economic difficulties which the Department of Transport must face.
Would the hon. member for Charlevoix allow me a question?
With pleasure.

Has the hon. member asserted, from what I heard when he discussed the

matter, that there was no flagrant contradiction between the statement of the Minister of Transport and the statement of the hon. member for Quebec East in the matter of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river?

I say there is no flagrant contradiction, because when the Minister of Transport made that statement on winter navigation on the St. Lawrence, he never promised to provide a regular escort to ships deciding to sail up the St. Lawrence to Quebec. He said he would do his very best to provide escorts for ships deciding to sail up to Quebec. I suggest that the hon. member go over the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Transport.
