speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate today, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man) on her very able presentation in seconding the motion in reply to the speech from the throne. I do this for a reason other than those previously mentioned. I am sure many of us are concerned by the fact that when we enter politics we give up many things for which we have the right to hope and one of these is an effective type of security for our wives if they should become widows. As we look around the country we find more and more politicians dying at an early age and leaving widows who have to fend for themselves. I am very pleased not only that the electors of her constituency saw fit to elect the hon. lady but that she is as capable as she is in making her presentation to the house. I hope that if my wife has to enter politics at any time because I have left her no future, she will receive as favourable a response as the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas has received in this house.
Like a number of other hon. members I am very concerned this year about the operations of the House of Commons itself. You will probably remember, Mr. Speaker, that at the end of last session I received many compliments for exercising the right to call it ten o'clock, but no doubt you would agree that the load of work which falls on the shoulders of a private member is considerably increased if the hours of sitting of the house are extended. I think that again we are facing exactly the same position as we were last year. If hon. members will look at the order paper they will see what has been put down on the order paper at the present time. They will find under government orders three or four fairly insignificant bills. One of them provides for the retirement of judges at the

age of 75. I am not disagreeing with the proposals in any of these bills. All I am saying is that they are insignificant. We are also to discuss an extension of grants that are made under the railway grade crossing fund for another three years. This arises because municipalities have been unable to take advantage of this particular provision, with the result that it is to be extended for another three years, the money provided in the past not having been spent.
Provision is being made to split up the Department of the Minister of Justice and give him two deputy ministers. That is all very good, perhaps, but it is not very important to the people of Canada. The last item on the order paper is a more important one; we are to add $500 million to the fund provided under the National Housing Act, bringing the total up from $1,000 million to $1,500 million.
Some of these measures may be important but it should be remembered that the speech from the throne mentioned a number of important matters that would be discussed, and I do not see any of these things on the order paper. What I am suggesting is that if they are important, and if we are running this place as a business as we should, the government should be prepared to bring in this type of legislation at the beginning of the session so that we may get on with it.
I have no objection to our finishing in three months, in four months or ten months. I have no objection how this is done. But I do suggest that a member of the house is dishonest if he sits here and lets the type of legislation to which I have referred be introduced and then, at the end of the session, brings in such things as crop insurance, a subject which was introduced in the dying days of the last session before the problem had been fully discussed in any of the provinces. In fact, by the end of the year most of the provinces had not even considered taking advantage of that legislation, or of implementing it. I am suggesting that debates on topics such as this should be undertaken early in the session and that parliament should be given a chance to do something about them. Otherwise, we would be less than honest if we did not recognize that someone was holding up the operations of this house.
I was very pleased that the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) mentioned some of these problems affecting our procedure. He made reference to some changes that he would like to see in operation; with some of his points, I agreed, though with others I did not. I do think, however, that he was drawing attention to a problem which
The Address-Mr. Peters should be seriously considered by all members of parliament. Yesterday, certainly we received what I might even call a lecture in which the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) outlined what he thought the House of Commons should be doing and the many improvements that could be introduced. Looking around the house yesterday and noting the silence which attended his remarks I thought that many hon. members held the same view as I do, namely that we should give a great deal more consideration to this very important topic.
There are so many of us here who are new to parliament and who have no experience of the tradition of parliament. We have to read the records in order to find out about that tradition. I think it is a disgrace the way in which some of the old-timers here play about with what they consider to be the tradition. We should make the House of Commons a more effective body and a more effective sounding board for public opinion. Backbenchers on all sides of the house are capable of making a far more effective contribution than is possible at present, but this contribution can only be made if the treasury benches enable it to be provided. In any case, if important pieces of legislation are held up until the end of the session when they cannot be properly discussed I think the people across Canada are right if they say we are not doing the job we were sent here to do.
I wish, now, to say a word about what is known as the private members' hour and to give notice that I may avail myself of the divorce procedure which we carry on here in order to bring this matter to the attention of the people across the country. Almost 400 of these divorce bills have been introduced already and if I were to ask for them to be handled separately in this house, without asking for a vote or any other consideration-simply that they be introduced separately, go into committee separately, and so on-as much time would probably be spent in this way as would be spent on all government legislation. Maybe we shall have to do this in order to focus attention on this particular matter. If this should be the case, I am quite willing to do it no matter who says it is wasting the time of the house, or whatever else people may want to say about it. Frankly, I do not care what most of the people say. I am interested in seeing that the operation of parliament is as effective as we could possibly make it, because we are now competing with other systems-other ideol-other things, Conservative members were ress, and if we cannot show that we can

The Address-Mr. Peters make the same kind of progress under democratic procedure, then, I suggest, people are going to give consideration to other ways of doing things.
There are, on the order paper, a number of important private members' bills. These bills are of great interest to the people who have introduced them as well as to large segments of the Canadian population and economy. Last year we found the government increasingly adopting the method of talking out bills sponsored by private members; talking them out without providing any leadership at all or indicating whether they agreed with the measure or whether they disagreed with it. I found it not unsatisfactory when-as happened in the case of one bill which I myself had the honour of introducing-the government states plainly that they cannot go along with it. In that case a vote was allowed and the bill was voted down. That was the right of the government and its supporters. But I am particularly concerned about those private bills which supporters of the government flogged to death. I would much prefer that the government opposed these bills and had the gumption to say: we shall call a vote. We do not believe in it. We do not think the time is right for this implementation, and we are willing to say so. If that happened, we could then get on with something else.
I suggest that it is clearly time private members' bills were given greater consideration by the government. Otherwise, someone like myself will say: very well, we will eliminate the whole process and discuss divorce for five or six months during the private members' hour. This would also eliminate some public bills which might be of concern to some parts of the country.
I am also concerned with regard to the question period. Many of the questions that are asked are sensible questions, but I am inclined to believe that many others which have been asked, particularly in the last day or two, are manipulations between certain people on both sides of this house. Simple questions are asked that require simple, direct answers. Occasionally an irrelevant statement that is out of order will be attached to the question. A minister of the crown will rise and respond to the irrelevancy and a lengthy discussion will ensue that is without meaning or value. I am suggesting that this is an affront to the Speaker and lessens the dignity of parliament without accomplishing anything. We can surely expect better conduct on the part of members of the house of long standing who should be willing to provide leadership to those of us who are new and are eager to learn about the effective operation of parliament.

I have no more respect for the way the Liberal administration operated than I have for the operation of the present administration but at least under the Liberals ministers would take under advisement the question that was advanced and reply in due course. It should not be considered that a member is automatically out of order in bringing forward a question. If he is sincere in wanting an answer he should not be ridiculed.
The hon. member for Port Arthur dealt with committee work in his address. I am not as well read as he is and I do not know what committees of parliament are supposed to do. Over the years, however, I have sat on many trade union committees and learned something about the way they operate. They are established for a specific purpose and when they have accomplished it they make a report through the body that appointed them. That body considers the report and either rejects or accepts the report or any portion thereof.
I did not agree entirely with the report brought in by the defence committee a year or two ago and would not have wanted some of its recommendations implemented. Nevertheless, that committee conducted a thorough investigation of the subject and made a splendid report. Nothing that has transpired since indicates to me that the government, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) or the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) gave any consideration to the recommendations of that committee. If the work of committees is to be ignored I see no reason for not abolishing them.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has great parliamentary experience and professes himself to be interested in the rights of parliament. I think it is disgraceful that he should consider the setting up of another committee when apparently he has no desire at all to implement the recommendations contained in the reports of any of the existing committees established under the rules of this house.
Committee work is important. It gives the little fellow a chance to have his say and make a valuable contribution. He is free to speak without thought of party consideration as a representative of his riding on a subject about which he may know a great deal. If committee reports are to be ignored parliament is cheating itself of these valuable contributions. It may be said that it has not been the policy over the years to implement committee recommendations and that may be true but there are approximately 200 of us who have not been here over the years. In the main, we are young and we want to see a good job done. If the older members do not provide leadership to us

and if John Diefenbaker who claims to defend the rights of parliament does not show some initiative in this regard, there will be many of us who simply will not run again because we can spend our time more effectively in other places.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member has referred to another hon. member of this house by name and that is forbidden under the practice of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member for Prince Albert will not be offended at my having used his name. I notice that this is not a Conservative government any longer as much as it is a Diefenbaker government, so I do not think that is a real point of order.

Order. Dealing with the point of order made by the hon. member for Halifax, he is quite correct in what he says. I would ask the hon. member who is now speaking to henceforth refer to the hon. gentleman in question as the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, which is the proper way, or as the hon. member for Prince Albert.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Consideration should be given to these matters at the beginning of the session and probably the throne speech debate is the time to do it. We have not considered what is to be the length of the session. I have heard it said in the corridors that we may wind up in June although others say it will be late in September. Is it not unfitting that we should have speculation as to the length of the session? Is it not the prerogative of the cabinet to consider the legislative program and the time allotted for its proper passage? I suggest the government could and should consider this question and announce the length of the session as each session begins.
I am not in agreement with those who say that being a member of parliament is a part-time job. I have found few hon. members who are able to augment their income from the job or profession they normally follow. This is also true of members of the legal profession some of whom over the years were able to conduct their law practice from the House of Commons. As a member of parliament I am prepared to work here nine or ten months out of the year and have recesses at regular times and operate on a full-time basis. I am sure many other hon. members are prepared to do that.
I offer no apology for the course followed by members of this group at the end of last session when we insisted on observing the rules of the house at a time when the
The Address-Mr. Peters government was attempting to rush through legislation that should not have been rushed through. I believe this is the time during the course of the session when we should resolve to order our business in such a way as to expedite our sittings.
The normal role of a backbencher like myself is to speak about matters concerning his constituency. In travelling around the country I have learned that the problems in my own constituency are those of Canadians in general, and so without listing the towns in my riding and their respective problems, I feel I can discuss these questions in broader terms.
One problem affecting Canadians greatly is agriculture. I was surprised that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) should have spoken for 40 minutes without getting around to saying the things I am sure he intended to say. I was also surprised that the Minister of Defence Production should have had to finish making his statement for him. No doubt this was an oversight. I agree that he should thank the Minister of Defence Production for speaking about the matter of deficiency payments for eggs and pork, because it is a matter that should have been brought to the attention of the house by the minister himself.
This problem has grown during the past days. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) mentioned this matter, as it concerned his riding. It was again brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden), both of whom represent farm ridings and understand that the problem as outlined by the minister is not a true picture at all. I am inclined to believe that the Financial Post of October 17 had a much better picture of what was going to happen to the egg situation when they headed an article, "Ottawa Quits the Egg Business". I would suggest that is exactly what they have done. Many farmers across the country will agree that Ottawa has quit the egg business and it is time they got back in with at least a limited support for eggs.
The Financial Post points out that the support program produced an unmanageable surplus of eggs, and they go on to say that therefore the government had to get out. Yesterday the hon. member for Rosthern pointed out that it was not the purpose of the deficiency payments to eliminate surpluses. This was part of the problem, and the problem had to be handled separately.
Some of the things that have been happening in the egg picture have been brought to the attention of the house. One of the decisions that the minister made was a sensible one. Over the period of the last two

The Address-Mr. Peters or three years the minister and all the members of the house have been much concerned with vertical integration. Vertical integration has produced a surplus of eggs and it has produced surpluses of many agricultural commodities. In the matter of putting a ceiling on the number of eggs that could be given assistance the minister was travelling along the right direction. He chose as a basis for deficiency payments the amount of 4,000 dozen eggs. This number appears to be the production from a flock of about 500 hens. This, I would suggest, is a small flock by Canadian standards, and therefore the flock should be raised by a considerable number. The ceiling should be there and should be maintained, however, because it will be one of the ways of eliminating the surplus created by vertical integration.
A number of articles have appeared in the papers which give rise to other problems concerning this matter of egg production. One of them is the problem that has been brought to the attention of the house on other occasions, namely that of chickens next year. The hatcheries made presentations stating that if the egg production continues to drop because there is no price for eggs, then we are going to be faced with a very serious shortage of hatchery eggs and that this in turn will raise the price of eggs to both the consumers and hatcheries in a year or possibly a year and a half.
Another problem that has been pointed out is that this does not seem to have had any effect on the wholesaler. It is pointed out in an article in the Regina Leader-Post of January 22 that grade A large eggs are giving the farmer a return of 14 cents; that the retailer is making 15 cents on them and the consumer is paying 33 cents to 34 cents. They also point out that it is worse in the field of medium eggs where there is no deficiency payment. The farmer is getting 12 cents and the retailer is getting 14 cents. It does not seem to make any difference how much the eggs are selling for, the retailer and wholesaler are getting their share out of handling this commodity, and the one who takes the cut is the farmer. I would suggest also that this matter was never discussed with members in a caucus of the Conservative party or, if it was, the minister again disregarded the advice of some of the backbenchers who are familiar with this problem. This is quite evident in the remarks that have been made concerning this problem in the debate so far.
We have another problem with regard to deficiency payments, and that is in the field of hogs. Pork is meeting the same problems that are evident in the case of eggs, and there are also other problems. In


my area over the years we sold to the local packer. The local packer used to come around and offer whatever he wished to the farmer, and if he did not sell to the packer, then he kept the pig and took whatever loss there was. In other words, he sold for whatever was offered to him because there was no other market.
Many of the farmers have banded together now and have established community sales. These community sales have been able to increase the price of pigs and other livestock. But because of the manner in which deficiency payments are made it has eliminated farmers from getting any kind of deficiency payments on pigs that are sold through community sales. It has meant that with respect to many of our people who want to protect themselves on deficiency payments they have had to go back to selling to the local packer and have taken a loss beyond what they might have had to take if they stayed with the community sales. The agriculture committee could quite easily devise some methods that would allow the farmer to continue to sell through the community sales and at the same time receive any benefits of federal legislation which would have accrued to him if he had sold in the normal way to the packing house.
In the last few days we have continually heard about money. I was interested to note that it is a matter that not only we on this side of the house discuss but the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), in his extended time, also went on to talk about money. I agree that he is one man who should talk about money because in the labour field we continually hear that the whole problem of increased resistance to sales on foreign markets and our losses in trade and other considerations have all been brought about by the fact that labour is getting increases in wages and pricing us out of our external markets. I think some of the members who have parroted this charge of many of the manufacturing concerns would do well to consider the things that the minister said this afternoon and relate them directly to the labour problem.
We have been very interested in this problem on this side of the house because we are aware of a number of things that have not been given much consideration. For one thing, there are two types of money in this country. It has been said there is tight money and, at the same time, it has been said that there is lots of money available. I believe that both of these statements are true. There is lots of money for certain investment and there is a very tight money policy for us who happen to borrow through

the banks or through the institutions which are controlled directly by the government through the Bank of Canada. We have heard of restrictions in this field where there is buying resistance or where extended credit is not allowed and at the same time fortunes are coming into this country, attracted by the extended potentialities that we have, which do not enter at all into the matters which are under the control of the Bank of Canada or, for that matter, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). This is of importance to quite a number of people. Wilfrid C. Krug, in an address to a joint meeting of the junior and senior boards of trade in Toronto on October 26 last, said:
Today money is tight and costly.
He went on to say:
If continued, it will result in a breakdown and an end to our system of private enterprise.
I think this matter should concern hon. members. Mr. Krug went on to say:
The premium encourages Canadians to spend money abroad and discourages foreigners from spending money in Canada.
1 represent a mining community where the people are very interested in this matter of money, particularly money coming into the country for the development of our natural resources and its relationship to the premium on the dollar. As hon. members know, when our mines sell their gold they sell it at $35 United States and the higher the Canadian dollar goes the less money the mines get for their gold and the less opportunity there is for these mining communities to continue their existence.
The Minister of Finance spoke in Toronto on Monday, January 11 and dealt with five suggestions having to do with reducing the premium on the dollar. I am particularly interested in the fifth one. I think the others are pretty much the same and can be dealt with in the same way. The minister said that he did not see any reason to increase the price of gold in Canada because this would immediately mean that we would have to pay more for gold coming from other sources. The minister had this to say:
To limit the payment of the increased price to Canadian-produced gold it would, of course, be necessary to prohibit the import of gold from outside Canada.
There is an implication here, that we are importing gold from outside Canada. If we are, I should like to ask the minister why we are and what is the purpose of our buying such gold. The minister said that if we adopted any one of the five suggestions we would immediately make the problem more difficult and increase the premium on the dollar instead of decreasing it or that if we
The Address-Mr. Peters went to the extreme and prohibited the importation of money from the United States and other countries then we would eliminate the entry of capital from the United States.
I am inclined to believe that in some cases this would not be a bad idea. A great deal of money is coming into Canada from the United States for investment in the development of natural resources and it is coming into this country for the very simple reason that these people can make a large capital gain and there is no tax on that gain. There is a capital gains tax of 25 per cent in the United States and I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if he would impose such a tax in Canada a great deal of this money would no longer continue to come into this country. If we are going to develop our natural resources by assisting people in another country to make 25 per cent more profit, then I think we should give consideration to the suggestion I have made and take a close look at the matter.
I should like to speak briefly about the uranium industry and the problems that have been created by the government in that industry. A brief was presented to the first Canadian conference on uranium and atomic energy by Larry Sefton, director of district 6, united steelworkers of America, on January 13 of this year and among other things he said:
In conclusion, let me suggest that the present crisis in uranium should teach us two lessons. In future, when some new area of natural resource exploitation opens up, let us have consultation between government, management and labour, not merely between government and investors, in advance-The uranium crisis should show us clearly that the interests of the people are just as important as the interests of capital and that, unless we plan to protect these interests in advance, the public may end up losing more out of exploitation of natural resources than they are worth.
I suggest that this sometimes happens in the development of our resources, and if we impose a capital gains tax we will eliminate the flow of money now being used to develop resources in instances where, as has proved to be the case in the uranium industry at Elliot Lake, it might be better if we had proceeded slowly and reached a concrete understanding of the problem before allowing development to proceed.
I should like to deal with the position of the civil service. It would seem to me that we have given very little consideration to our civil servants. I am not going to mention all the ways that we have tried to protect our civil servants without allowing them to have unions. A commission was appointed by government and it laid down a set of ground rules under which the civil service is supposed to operate, but I wish to suggest that we want to maintain the highest level of efficiency we can with the least number of
532	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Peters civil servants. I suggest that the government is going to have to give consideration to the manner in which civil service associations are set up, the relationship that the government has with such associations and also the question of whether we are getting the most we can out of our civil service.
I think we can afford to pay a sizeable increase to civil servants. I also suggest that we dispense with a number of civil servants and I think consideration should be given to that point. I am of the opinion that civil servants differ in no way from any other kind of employee. I think the only difference is that civil servants bargain with the government and therefore under our labour legislation machinery should be set up under which they can bargain. I suggest there is nothing wrong with civil servants having available to them the full process of collective bargaining and I have no objection to them taking strike action if that seems to be necessary.
Some people will say that this is not what we want for our civil servants but I would suggest there is only one alternative and that is for civil servants to get into politics and decide who the government is going to be. We are having enough trouble with some of the senior civil servants now interfering in government but I suggest that civil servants should not have to try to change the government just because they want to get a wage increase.
I think what happened in Russell riding is a good example of civil servants becoming interested in politics and making their voice heard. I think it would be wise to consider what happened there before it grows to the point where it affects all civil servants, and I think we should give them the bargaining rights which they deserve.
I want to use one example. I have received a great number of letters from postal employees in my area. They are civil servants and they have an association. They are connected with other similar associations across Canada and are organized in a national organization and belong to the Canadian Labour Congress. There are three particular organizations to which they belong and in point of fact they are unions. These men are also civil servants and they receive no consideration because the same problem affects the whole civil service and because of the fact that we have not separate methods of negotiation for wage increases from the government.
The machinery is there. The government has the opportunity of putting it into effect and giving these people a voice. This does not mean that every time civil service matters are discussed they must be thrown in with the R.C.M.P., the army, navy, air force and all the other organizations that come under


the government. They should be treated as civil servants and where wages are concerned every consideration should be given to them that is given to people who are not civil servants.
In closing I should like to mention the case of one postal employee who has to deliver to 700 homes. When he has a piece of literature from a soap company to deliver he has to call at each of these 700 homes and yet he is only paid $240 a month.
I might suggest to the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) that he might solve a great many of the problems if they were paid more money in that service and he would not have to answer questions such as those he has been asked in the last few days.

Mr. Speaker, my first words may I direct to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I was sorry to interrupt him in his speech but he showed such zeal for the rights and privileges of parliament that I thought he would appreciate it if I pointed out that he was offending against one of the oldest rules of practice that we have.
May I express through you, Mr. Speaker, to your new deputy my most fervent congratulations on his acclamation to that position, an honour which I am sure he will reflect on behalf of the whole house. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I must say a few words for the hon. member who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I had the pleasure of accompanying the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) on a trip to Paris in the fall of 1958 when we attended the UNESCO conference. I must praise the wonderfull job he did in the administrative committee.
Furthermore, I know that his speech was excellent because since then I heard strong protests on the part of Quebec Liberal members.
(Text):
May I also congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) who so ably seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have heard, on the hon. lady's authority, that these were all her own ideas although, when we were listening to them, I thought some of them seemed to be the ideas of some political philosophers of the past. For example, she laid upon the word "work" and the idea of work as an emphasis that has not been heard in very recent times. I imagine that part of her understanding and her background could have been owing to her father who also sits in this house, and I am sure that she had a proper upbringing.

The Address-Mr. McCleave
I have some kind words for the new ministers, and the parliamentary secretaries who are already ascending those Olympic heights to even greater glory, and I wish a welcome to the new members at this session.
May I also say something about the marathon speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)-a discourse of some two hours and forty seven minutes, according to my timing-which would make one marvel at first blush at the ability of anybody to carry on for so long. But I have finally decided just why he was able to do so at such length. It is extremely easy to see the goal in sight if you are running around in a very narrow circle.
The Leader of the Opposition has a facility for the gifted phrase; and as he threw some gratuitously at our party I think it would be proper if somebody replied in kind. Here is a program for liberalism which I offer freely to the party or, as it is now designated, the group: labour for laissez faire; ideas for inventions; backbone for boloney; energy for excitement; realism for rancour; ability for arrogance; and liberal for lackadaisical.
Lest anybody quarrel with the depth or lack of depth of feeling behind those words, I will be the first to admit that it is perhaps a very small formula and to offer to the Leader of the Opposition another phrase, as he is very fond of phrases: "People who live in glass houses shouldn't".
As I look around the Leader of the Opposition at the four horsemen of the Apocalypse I notice one who is concerned now with turning his party into a group. I believe this is simply an unconscious wish on his part that he in time may take over the leadership of a group a little further to his left, politically speaking.
May I now turn to more serious matters and consider first the problem of radioactive fallout in our time. This matter has been dealt with at the United Nations and perhaps, subsequently in the debate on external affairs I shall have an opportunity to speak about the decisions that were reached by that body last fall. As most hon. members, if not all, are aware, owing to Canadian initiative-for which we must give due thanks to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) - Canada was able to initiate a resolution which won world-wide approval at the United Nations. This success entailed a considerable amount of work. For one thing, the suspicions of the soviets and their followers had to be cleared aside. For another thing, when you try to get 82 countries or 83 countries to agree, you will find each one throwing its
own particular ideas into the pot. But after some 36 drafts of a resolution one was finally adopted which will provide for joint studies to stimulate the flow of information and data on fallout and radiation levels and for encouraging genetic biological and other studies on the effects of radiation exposure on the health of human beings everywhere. No country is immune to radioactive fallout.
I do not intend to pursue the course followed by Canada at the United Nations, but I have some thoughts about the status of this rather serious problem in our own country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs in his remarks to the United Nations pointed out that even with an end to nuclear testing the problem of ionizing radiation will still exist. He went on to say this:
There will continue for several years to be fallout of radioactive particles already in the atmosphere. There will also be long term effects from the movement of radioactive isotopes through food chains. Even more important, there will continue to be for a long time genetic and biological effects from radiation, both man-made and natural, on the health of human populations.
In short, the gist of the problem is that even with a cessation of nuclear testing the amount of these invisible particles which bombard us every moment of our lives will increase in intensity over the next few years before a decrease begins. One scientist I know estimates that the amount of radiation will increase until the year 1966 and then decrease so that by the year 2,000 we shall have reached the position in which we are at present.
One can also see that if nuclear testing should be resumed by the large powers one would reach perhaps the danger line about which I will say a word in a few moments' time. It was therefore gratifying to me personally-and I am sure to every Canadian- to know of the strong stand taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of this country in the United Nations and at other international conferences to prevent nuclear testing and to show that Canada as a whole is united against the resumption of such tests.
I mentioned a possible danger point. The language of the scientists who deal with this subject is filled with such jargon as "maximum permissible concentration", known vulgarly in that trade as "mpc". It is true that in Canada, according to the figures, all parts of the country are well below the maximum permissible concentration recently established as a safety factor by the international commission on radiological protection, and much further below the previous figure recommended by that same commission somewhat earlier. There is, however, one city in Canada that is just under the

The Address-Mr. McCleave latest limit proposed by the international commission on radiological protection as the maximum permissible concentration. The amounts, of course, of radiation tend to vary quite rapidly, so that while that particular locality in Canada was close to the limit in one month, a few months later the figure would decrease very substantially below the limit.
Of course, one should realize that the mpc, the formula I have mentioned, is rather like a safety limit which says that you should not drive at 100 miles an hour forever, for if you do drive at 100 miles an hour forever, somewhere along the way you are most likely to be killed. In short, one can go through the mpc for a short period of time, but one cannot live forever in an area or city where the amount of radiation has surpassed the maximum permissible concentration and then has remained above that safety limit.
My purpose in mentioning this at some length is to bring this suggestion to the government. During the past year there has been a considerable interest among the science professors in universities on this problem of the hazards of radioactivity, and from time to time different universities have sent forward petitions or documents to the government against the resumption of nuclear testing. There is no need, of course, to petition the government on that; the government is firmly committed against nuclear testing.
I thought that the universities might be able to play a more useful role, because these men in their ivory towers hovering over their test tubes, counters and meters are not politically minded, but rather can be said to have a dispassionate regard for the welfare of mankind. It would seem to me that the Department of National Health and Welfare should be able to summon together the talents of these university professors and have some sort of full scale conference so that a proper document or some proper information can be compiled to enlighten the public. I think it is fair to say from reading about it that the amount of radiation in Canada is not a threat to mankind, but we do from time to time have statements from professors who are not fully conversant with that particular field of study but who are probably regarded by Canadians as some kind of authority. So I make that suggestion. I also welcome the establishment last year at H.M.C.S. Shearwater in my riding of a new station by the Department of National Health and Welfare which will monitor the amount of radioactivity in air and rainfall. This is one of 24 such stations across Canada.
A few days ago in this house, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), who reports to us on behalf of the Canadian

Broadcasting Corporation, announced the appointment of W. E. S. Briggs of Halifax as vice president and general manager of the C.B.C. The throne speech contains the information that the radio committee of the House of Commons will be in action again this year. I hope that Captain Briggs will be given a suitable amount of time to settle down in his new job in central Canada before being called before the committee.
I would venture the suggestion that his first and most important job is to restore the morale of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It seems to me that the lack of morale, for whatever reason, was clearly shown last year from certain events, not only before our committee but outside; for example, the strike in French Canada, and when certain talks producers followed certain talks producers in Toronto like a group of lemmings over an apparent cliff and out of their jobs. However they managed to scramble back up the cliff and to the safety of their pay cheques before anything serious happened to them. But it seemed to me, from watching events in the radio committee of the commons last year, that on any occasion where difficult points arose you could see the C.B.C. shaking like a mould of very poorly constructed jelly. In short, there was nothing in the way of a fibre of morale which seemed to hold the organization together.
I do not think that condition came about in just one year. I think the disease, or the cause of it, came about a long time back. For example, we were presented with one statistic which to me was very revealing, namely that in some 15 years only one employee of the C.B.C. had ever been fired for inefficiency. If you average it out at 7,000 employees for that 15-year period, and only one of these men is given the bounce for inefficiency, then we find that the workingman-year-odds that he cannot be fired from the C.B.C. are something like 104,999 to one. No other industry in Canada could ever possibly do that sort of thing.
I suggest that the corporation's whole morale would be brightened considerably and perked up if some of the inefficient people were shown through a one way door to the street, and then the efficient people could see that the C.B.C. was, after all, something in which they could take a great deal more pride. I know that Captain Briggs can give his attention to a subject such as that because of his outstanding record with the navy over some 30 years. It would always have been his objective there, I know, to see that he had what is called "a good ship". I know that now the C.B.C. is in his hands it will turn out to be a good radio and television broadcasting enterprise.

Suggestions have been made about changes in the rules of the house, and I was interested in the comments of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) that the Clerk of the house conduct a school so that members would learn what questions to ask and how to conduct themselves at all times. I presume that the first people that would be sent to the school would be those along the front benches immediately to my right. In any event, Mr. Speaker, we hope that we can be spared. You have shown a deftness in keeping certain members away from the area of robberies in post offices. If you had not done that I would have despaired because I could see some day a trend developing where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would be asked about robberies in banks.

The four horsemen of the Apocalypse have been joined by a fifth riding on his donkey.
Mr. Speaker, I turn now to a matter which gave some concern to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) when he spoke about the large numbers of divorce cases which are handled in the House of Commons and the other place. It so happens that today's votes and proceedings are considerably fattened by the addition of some 324 names of petitioners for bills of divorce before this house.
It is not my intention now to speak about the need for divorce reform in matters of substance, that is, broadening the grounds from adultery to include homosexuality and other sexual perversions, though it does seem to me that there is a need for parliament to recognize the wisdom of taking this course at some time. I should like to make some comments about the particular rules of the house itself so that we may deal with divorce more efficiently.
Last year, in the dying days of the session, I presented a report on behalf of the miscellaneous private bills committee in which we asked to be given at this session certain rules which would help set forth some procedure. These will be very similar to the rules that are drawn up by judges- rules of the court-and I hope that at some time during this session the government will respond to the wishes of that particular committee and, perhaps, direct that the committee on standing orders be seized with this chore of drawing up rules of assistance in handling these divorce cases. I know that I myself and the law counsel to the house besides a goodly number of members-I would name them all but they are ten or 15 in number and all of them have
The Address-Mr. McCleave ideas-could appear before the committee on standing orders and present a few interesting suggestions for changes.
One obvious need, for example, is to set a time limit for the right to appeal. When the other place has passed a divorce, when it comes before us and when it has been contested in the other place, the respondent party should have either a week or two weeks or ten days in which to notify the House of Commons of the intention to appeal. That seems obvious, yet we lack that power. As a matter of fact, we do not have any rules at all.
The second matter is probably the establishment of the principle of res judicata. I notice that this year a case has come before parliament for the third year in a row. The first year it came into the House of Commons and on the very last day of the session, or on the day previous to that, thanks to the democratic spirit of those in the group of eight, it was talked out, so that a man who had come before parliament asking for justice was, in effect, deprived of justice. They could have said yes to him, or no to him, by voting. Instead, that man was cast aside on the personal whim of a few people. I do not want to rake over the past, but that was perhaps the most sickening travesty of justice that I have seen in my few years in parliament. This man came before parliament again last year. On that occasion he was not successful in going through the Senate. Now he is trying again this year. Whatever my feelings about the merit of this man's case and the shabby treatment that he received thanks to the members of the C.C.F. in the House of Commons, I still do not think it is proper that a man whose case has been disposed of in a particular year should bring that case forward again. The first year did not count, because there was no effective disposition one way or the other in the House of Commons, but last year there was an effective disposition in the Senate, so the principle of res judicata is one that must be considered.
The third matter will be dealt with in the other house, I am informed by the chairman of the committee there, but it is one to which we should put our minds. It frequently happens that a wife will defend a divorce because under the rules it is required that the husband should give her money so that she may hire a lawyer to attack his case. Once that money has been duly passed over, by order of parliament, it often happens that the wife will pocket it and disappear. This is a somewhat elegant form of female Robin Hoodery-perhaps making the last touch upon her husband's purse. Nevertheless, we should combat anything like that. The hon.

The Address-Mr. McCleave senator in charge of the proceedings in the other house has taken the initiative to cure this practice but it is something that we in turn should consider curing here.
May I turn, now, to some purely local matters. Yesterday, the Canadian Labour Congress appeared before the government and presented its views in a brief which I am sure is known to most hon. members. I should like to mention one of these submissions. It concerns the dockyard in Halifax where for some time a goodly number of prevailing rate employees-at least 4,000-have been anxious to establish some form of check-off on their dues. This has been denied in the past and, when I say the past I mean the past going back a great number of years. So the Canadian Labour Congress has made a request of the government that these people's wish that they belong to organizations other than the association and the national joint council of the public service of Canada be respected. I think it would be a very simple matter to determine these people's wishes. The president of the Halifax dockyard labour council assured me that they would set up the machinery for a vote at any time and see that it was properly carried out, and I hope the government will go for a change in this policy which I think discriminates against groups and makes labour unhappy and which could be cured simply.
One of the outstanding achievements of the government to my mind has been something which has passed almost unnoticed; it slipped by in the dying days of the last session of parliament. That was the decision by the government to establish an institute of oceanography on the Bedford basin in Halifax county. This decision was announced in the house by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) on July 17 of last year and I hope he will be sufficiently thanked by the people of Canada as a whole for his imagination in establishing this institute which will deal with oceanography and also stimulate geology. Its purpose will be to help develop resources and also to find out useful information for continental defence. This institute is working in collaboration with Dalhousie University-one of our great universities-which is establishing a department that will fit in with the institute.
May I mention that another university, the oldest English-speaking university in Canada, King's College, is anxious to get into the field of a Latin-American institute. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) will be equally as imaginative as the Minister of Mines and


Technical Surveys when they come forth with their request.
There are other matters, including the need for some form of permanent building for the reserve navy in Halifax. It may seem odd that one should make such a request here considering the very large resources that the regular navy have there but apparently all hands are agreed, both regulars and reservists, that the reservists should have buildings separate and apart from naval establishments and in fact the duty that is incumbent on the reserve navy to provide so many trained men at an instant's notice should there be an outbreak of hostilities makes the need very apparent.
Finally, a bit of philosophy on the over-all approach, as I see it, of the maritimes to the rest of Canada and its development. I do not think that any of us from the maritimes, whether Conservative or Liberal in our thinking or outlook, are "aginners" or against the march of progress that has taken place in the rest of Canada. I do not think any one of us would want to say to the rest of Canada, "Stay back until we have caught up with you". But from the maritime members I have heard speak I believe the approach is, "Help us to progress, keep on going yourselves, and eventually we will catch up with you."

Order. Order.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member for St. James rose on a question of privilege concerning the Russell by-election. He has just mentioned that the member for St. Ann was there. You can be sure that I was there.

The Address-Mr. Loiselle
When we were asked to take part in the election campaign in Russell, it was because all the Conservative forces were already there, about thirty members headed by seven ministers.
What happened then is that a handful of Liberals came to the help of the Liberal candidate. Besides, I know that the member for St. James (Mr. Campeau) brought along seven or eight of his friends. We had to face a Conservative army, as well as another one, that of the Union Nationale from the province of Quebec.
You know the results, Mr. Speaker: the majority jumped from 2,000 to 7,000 votes.
Instead of raising the question of privilege, the hon. member for St. James should have moved a motion of congratulations to us.
Mr. Speaker, I should like, at the beginning of my remarks, to congratulate both the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Morissette and Mrs. Casselman).
I realize they were obligated to defend their party, so that their speeches could be nothing else but paeans of praise to a government which, in my opinion, deserves none.
The mover, the hon. member for Rimouski, tried to make us believe that everything is going well, that the financial situation in Canada is good, and that this government has been the most prosperous one for a long time.
I would not like him to believe, Mr. Speaker, that he has fooled all members, because only the indifferent and those who do not want to face facts can claim he is right.
With regard to the charming representative of Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), who seconded the motion, she spoke glowingly of her constituency of Grenville-Dundas and said how happy she is to represent that part of our country.
I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, to see you again, at the beginning of this session, fulfilling the functions which were entrusted to you after the 1958 election.
I must also congratulate the representative of the constituency of Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) for earning the confidence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has appointed him Associate Minister of National Defence.
As everyone knows, the speech from the throne is prepared by the cabinet, and the Governor General is asked to read it officially, in order that Canadian citizens may be informed of the government's intentions and projects to be submitted to the house.
This year, contrary to tradition and parliamentary practice, there has not been only one speech but two, one by the Governor General and the other by the Prime Minister.
As to the speech read by the Governor General, it could have contained many things of vital importance to the Canadian population rather than a report on the international situation during the last months, and the mere mention of a few bills.
There is the announcement that the Prime Minister will make a trip next May, in order to meet other government heads of the commonwealth. The Prime Minister might have saved himself the trouble of announcing his trip in the speech from the throne, as we are now used to seeing him travel quite frequently from one country to another. In the same paragraph of the speech, we are given the news, which we read in the papers sometime ago, that Nigeria would become an independent member.
In the two following paragraphs, we are told about a meeting of the leaders of the four nations with a view to establishing durable peace in the world, of disarming and abolishing nuclear tests. And so it goes on, Mr. Speaker, for in the whole first part of the speech from the throne, we are only told about international problems.
In the second part, some of our own issues are mentioned, and also what has been accomplished-that is to say the things that should be done in certain fields; there is a mention of some bills which the house will be asked to pass in the near future.
But, as far as the deplorable problem of unemployment is concerned, there is just one little sentence turned in such a way that one could be led to think that everything is well, or nearly so, in the employment field.
Now this is what our executive has to say about prevailing conditions. I shall actually quote the speech from the throne:
The recurrent problem of seasonal unemployment remains, however, but apart from this, expansion in production and employment has been general across the nation.
That is all the government has to say on unemployment. That is all the comfort and encouragement being given to the 685,000 people who were out of jobs in December. Now, according to the figures supplied this afternoon by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the unemployment figure had reached 755,387 on January 14. This means that unemployment increased by 70,000 from December 31 to January 14, and according to present trends, it would come as no surprise if, by the end of December, the figure rose above
538	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Loiselle 800,000. Yet in his speech this afternoon, the Minister of Labour made no reference to any government action aimed at checking unemployment.
He quoted figures for 1954, 1955 and 1956, and even quoted United States figures. I hardly know, Mr. Speaker, how the 100,000 unemployed people in Montreal would react if they could hear the same speech be made this afternoon in the heart of Montreal; with an audience of 100,000 unemployed, I am sure the reaction would be quite violent.
The Prime Minister, in making his own speech from the throne and in announcing three important measures which are nothing but political propaganda, certainly showed little consideration for the queen's representative in Canada, and showed how little he cares for the rights and prerogatives of parliament despite the way he used to champion them when sitting as a solitary member of the opposition.
In his speech, which rambled on for over three hours, the Prime Minister vainly attempted, by means of a long series of quotations, to show contradictions in various statements on national defence made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). However, he forgot to deal with his government's policy in this field which is of such important concern to every Canadian.
Near the end of his speech he touched upon the economic picture but made no reference to the grave difficulties we now face both in the fields of trade and agriculture and in matters of money and finance.
Here again, he gave us a whole string of quotations from Canadian bankers, but at no time did he refer to the disturbing number of people suffering from unemployment in Canada. Yet it is this same man who travelled throughout Canada in the last elections, telling voters that no one would suffer from unemployment while he was Prime Minister. Now that the leader of the Conservative party has succeeded in fooling the voters with irresponsible promises, he has completely forgotten Canada's unemployed people. Yet their numbers keep growing day by day.
During 1959, an average of over 6 per cent of our workers were in search of employment, according to the federal bureau of statistics. Apart from 1958, this is the highest rate ever experienced since the famous depression.
The province of Quebec has the dubious honour of having the greatest number of unemployed in Canada. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, on December


12, 1959, there were 370,000 unemployed in Canada, 136,000 of them in Quebec, and only
98.000	in Ontario where the population is even greater than in Quebec. That goes to show that in December 1959, almost 37 per cent of unemployed in Canada lived in the province of Quebec.
But that is not all, because the statistics published by the Department of Labour are even more disturbing and also most likely closer to the truth. On December 31, 1959, there were 685,000 unemployed in Canada in comparison with 715,000 in December 1958, which is a decrease of 25,000 only.
As I was saying a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, since those figures were published in the bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics, the Minister of Labour has informed us that on January 14, the number of unemployed stood at 685,000, whereas it stands today at 755,397, that is an increase of 70,000 within 14 days.
Here again, Quebec leads all the provinces with 221,000 unemployed in December 1959 in comparison with 231,000 in 1958, a decrease of 10,000 only. And yet, the government would like the people to believe that, in comparison with the 1958 recession, we are now experiencing a record prosperity.
I am sure that the Quebec Conservative members of parliament who in the course of this debate have praised the government for our so-called state of prosperity would not dare repeat the same praises in the presence of their own people in their respective constituencies, and certainly not before the
100.000	unemployed of the city of Montreal.
Indeed, Montreal is the city where unemployment is heaviest at the present time. On November 30, 1959 there were, according to the Department of Labour, 53,855 unemployed in Montreal and 38,730 only in Toronto. Those are the latest figures available, but I am sure that at the present time, on the basis of statistics issued by the Department of Labour, the number of unemployed, as I said a moment ago, is well over 100,000 in the city of Montreal alone.
Consequently we have every reason to say that the unemployment problem is no doubt a serious one for our country and particularly in the province of Quebec and in the city of Montreal. What does the government intend to do to meet that problem and find work for the unemployed? Absolutely nothing; because the winter works program of the Department of Labour is nothing but a farce, particularly in the province of Quebec.

The minister indeed proved to us in his remarks this afternoon, that the winter projects program will give jobs to only 36,000 people in Canada, whereas we have 755,000 unemployed.
Not only has the government done nothing to solve the problem, but it seems to be doing its best to aggravate it. Indeed, because of tight money conditions and high interest rates, for which the government is fully responsible, home building has decreased in 1959 in comparison to 1958, and a further decline is foreseen in 1960. Moreover the government which, according to a statement made by the Prime Minister on July 22 last, was to maintain the availability of funds to builders until December 31, 1959, announced, on October 30, 1959, through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) that these loans would be suspended, without further notice, as from the day of his statement, that is two months before the date mentioned by the Prime Minister himself.
This is a further instance of the contradictions and irresponsibility, which are so characteristic of this government. But the real victims of the government's contradictions and financial difficulties, are the unemployed who, following the decline in the building industry caused by the government's policies, have lost their jobs and today live in misery.
Thus, it can be seen that far from finding a solution to the unemployment problem, the government through its disastrous policy tends to make it worse. It could even be said that the government goes as far as ignoring the existence of this tragedy. In his speech the Prime Minister made no mention about it and to my knowledge not one Conservative member from Quebec raised the problem, either to deplore it or to ask the government to take drastic action at once to solve it.
It seems to me that this problem has taken such proportions that it should not give rise to partisanship in this house. Before defending the Conservative party, government members must defend the legitimate interests of their constituents. That is why it is their duty to join us in this debate in asking the government that made so many promises before the election, to fulfill some of them and above all to assist those who suffer from unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, it is so true that the government or the crown corporations are not concerned about unemployment, that last week end, when I was in my riding, some employees of the Pointe St. Charles plants of the C.N.R., assured me that from 300 to
The Address-Mr. Loiselle 400 employees were to be laid off in the very near future. I was moreover informed that 700 or 1000 employees working in all C.N.R. plants were to be given notice.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, this is the same government which, with much publicity and many advertisements saying "Do it now" asks private builders and contractors to give work to our unemployed, but does not act itself in the matter. I think that the government should practise what it preaches. If private enterprise is asked to employ the jobless, the government should make its own contribution by giving an illustration of how to "Do it now".
Mr. Speaker, I said a few moments ago that this government has not given any evidence of good will nor submitted any projects to put a stop to prevailing unemployment conditions.
I would urge the government and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to introduce a resolution to the house, in order that members may be given the opportunity of discussing this situation which is deteriorating from day to day. Mr. Speaker, if I insist on that matter, it is because I represent a constituency essentially made up of workers.
I could outline to you the awful and difficult situation which now prevails in my constituency, as it affects unemployed people, some of them having been in that situation for a long time. Those people are now getting no unemployment insurance benefits; I would ask the government to show some good will and take the necessary steps to help those poor workers and heads of families.
Mr. Speaker, to prove my statements concerning unemployment

and the figures I have quoted, should not be taken only as a matter of criticism on the part of a member of the opposition-allow me to quote a few paragraphs of an article published in La Presse of January 20, 1960, that is, only about nine days ago. Dealing with the general unemployment situation, here is what it says:
Only a few weeks ago, in their end-of-the-year reviews or new-year messages, federal and provincial ministers promised prosperity to everyone, with an optimism which each one of us only asks to share. But, unfortunately, the latest statistics about unemployment, published yesterday, put such optimism to a cruel test. And those are only for the beginning of winter, since they only cover the period from mid-November to mid-December. And the gloomier part of the picture is in connection with the province of Quebec.
To put it briefly, the number of unemployed has increased by 90,000 during that period, to reach 370,000 in the country as a whole, and 136,000 in our province only. We therefore have the dubious honour of having over a third of Canada's unemployed.

The Address-Mr. Loiselle
Mr. Speaker, what strikes me most is that in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, so far no Conservative members from the province of Quebec have mentioned the word unemployment, or the fact that there are unemployed people in their respective constituencies. Surely, the
136,000	unemployed people living in Quebec are not restricted to Liberal constituencies, and a good many of them must live in the 50 constituencies represented by Conservative members. Mr. Speaker, I charge Conservative members who have remaind silent about unemployment conditions with neglecting to protect the interests of their constituents.
Mr. Speaker, the article to which I referred a moment ago goes on to say this:
We get strange statements from official sources.
Mention is made there of statements of ministers. I would urge you to listen very attentively because they are not my words but those of the author of the article:
Thus, according to the article published yesterday, the seasonal decrease in employment was counterbalanced (in Ontario not in Quebec, it is pointed out) "by a speeding up in plants previously affected by a lack of steel". Well, is it not a fact that federal ministers kept on telling us, all through the steel strike in the United States, that steel reserves were sufficient in Canada and that production stoppage among our neighbours had not affected our industry and our labour in this country? When should we accept official statements? When they say that a strike in the United States does not affect us or when they say that the end of such a strike results in a recovery in this country?
And the article concludes:
The truth is that there were close to 400,000 workers completely unemployed, and almost as many partly unemployed in mid-December. That makes over 750,000 Canadians working part time or totally unemployed. That was the situation prevailing at the very beginning of the winter. And the trend had a long way to go before reaching its peak.
With all this, what has happened to the famous winter works program so often mentioned by the federal Minister of Labour? It gave little relief last year.
And now, nothing more is said about it. There was not a slightest mention of it in the speech from the throne in which, on the other hand, there was only passing reference to unemployment just as if it did not exist.

When will the government wake up to reality?
Mr. Speaker, I read a few excerpts from this article in order to show the real situation as far as unemployment is concerned in our country and more particularly in the province of Quebec, since the Conservative members from that province will take no heed of it.
Several members of the Liberal party have mentioned it, and I am happy to associate myself with their remarks in that connection. For my part, I can assure you that I know the workers of the constituency of St. Ann, and that I shall defend their interests here as long as I shall be able to do so.
